summary: Kitto x features an attribute-based routing system inspired by MARS / WiRL, the popular Delphi REST libraries. Handler classes are decorated with custom Delphi attributes; the framework discovers them via RTTI at startup and dispatches HTTP requests to the matching method automatically.
text:
Attribute-Based Routing (RTTI)

 Kitto x features an attribute-based routing system inspired by MARS / WiRL, the popular Delphi REST libraries. Handler classes are decorated with custom Delphi attributes; the framework discovers them via RTTI at startup and dispatches HTTP requests to the matching method automatically.

This architecture enables:
 Extensibility — applications register custom URL handlers without modifying the framework
 Modularity — each feature (chart, calendar, map) lives in its own unit with zero coupling to the core
 Enterprise separation — enterprise modules can be included or excluded by simply adding/removing a reference

 How it works

 1. Declare a handler class

A handler is a plain Delphi class decorated with on the class (base path) and on each public method (sub-path). HTTP method attributes ( , ) specify which requests the method handles.

 warning RTTI directive required
The directive is mandatory in every handler unit. Without it, Delphi does not emit attribute metadata for methods and parameters, and the routing engine cannot discover the handler.

 2. Register the handler

Registration happens in the section — the same pattern used by for UI controllers:

At registration time, scans the class via RTTI:
1. Reads from the class → base path ( )
2. For each public method with + → creates a 
3. For each parameter → reads , , , or 
4. Sorts all registered handlers by specificity (more literal segments = higher priority)

 3. Request dispatch

When a request arrives, the engine (created per-request):
1. Matches the URL against all registered path templates — literal segments match exactly, segments capture any value
2. Fills method parameters from the appropriate source:
 - → extracted from the URL path
 - → from the query string ( )
 - → from the POST body
 - → resolved by type from the injection registry
3. Invokes the method via 
4. Cleans up — the handler instance is created and destroyed within the same request

 Per-request context

The attribute router is evaluated before the legacy request handler in the route chain: a matched request is served by the handler, while an unmatched one falls through to the legacy routing — so the two coexist as built-in endpoints are progressively migrated to attribute routing.

Before invoking the method, the framework activates the same per-request context as the legacy pipeline (the authenticator, access controller and macro engine are made current), then runs the dispatch through the shared request filter chain described below. So a handler can rely on , and being fully populated — including the correct active database when the app uses multiple databases — exactly as a legacy handler would.

 Request filters

Cross-cutting concerns — JWT session hydration, the authentication gate and error handling — are not coded inside each handler. They live in a filter chain that wraps the dispatch of both the attribute pipeline and the legacy request handler, so the behaviour is defined once and applied uniformly.

A filter implements :

attributes set, to short-circuit the dispatch, and — the name of
the view the request resolved to, or when the endpoint is not view-scoped. The imposed-step
gate below is built on that last one, and a custom filter can use it to reason per view without
re-parsing the URL.

Filters are registered globally with . Registration order = nesting: the first registered filter is the outermost layer (its runs first, its runs last). A filter's can fully satisfy the request (e.g. write a 404) by setting , which short-circuits the dispatch.

title: Introduction
summary: This document explains some basic concepts common to all Kitto x applications. Start here if you want to explore the examples in some depth and start creating your own applications.
text:
Introduction 

This document explains some basic concepts common to all Kitto x applications. Start here if you want to explore the examples in some depth and start creating your own applications.

 Structure of project files 

A Kitto x application is made up of

 a Delphi project;
 a set of metadata files;
 a set of resources.

 Metadata files 

Most of a Kitto x application lies in the metadata files.
All metadata files are in yaml format. Yaml is a human-readable markup language which is easier to read and less noisy and error-prone to write than XML or JSON, meaning that you can just open and edit the files in your preferred text editor. Just remember:

 A yaml file is a tree of nodes, each on its own text line with a name followed by a colon followed by a value.
 Valid data types for values include numbers, strings, dates but also space-separated lists and special values or macros. Multi-line values are supported as well.
 Indentation in yaml is paramount to define structure. Kitto x , by convention, uses two spaces for each level of indentation.
 Don't use tabs, only spaces. Kitto x refuses to parse files containing tabs.

Example:

As you can see in the example above, characters denote comments, while blank lines are ignored. StreetName and Number are child nodes of Address, which is a note with no value, just the children. Each value's data type is inferred by parsing it, and node names are case insensitive.

In the documentation and, as you'll see, in Delphi code, you can access nodes by path. A path is a string with hierarchy represented by slashes. In the example above, the node would be referred to as .

As mentioned above, you can break up long string values into multiple lines, by using a special introducer character as the node value and putting the text, indented, in the following lines:

The multi-lihe values continue until the text is outdented again. You can also use the > introducer. the difference between the two is as follows:

 The pipe ( ) preserves formatting (line breaks and spaces).
 The symbol does not preserve formatting, putting everything together.

 Macros 

 Kitto x supports macros, in the form of strings surrounded by %s, just about everywhere, and particularly in yaml values. See this page for a list of available macros and instructions on how to add your own.

 Metadata directory structure 

The Metadata directory contains one or more config files (by default, one called Config.yaml) and some subdirectories with more yaml files. Currently you have:

 Models containing one yaml file for each model, which is basically the representation of a database table (although it can be more abstract than that).
 Views containing one yaml file for each view, which is a piece of user interface, often linked to an underlying model or family of models.

Whenever you change a metadata file while the application is running, the change is visible to all new web sessions but not currently running session. You can restart the Kitto x server to close all sessions and force the change to be seen by everyone. This is done particularly often during development, as it's a button click in Kitto x 's control panel.

You only need to restart the Kitto x server when you recompile it, that is if you change any Delphi code inside it.

 Convention Over Configuration 

Now is a good time to mention that Kitto x favours convention over configuration (CoC) whenever possible, meaning that each setting can be done at different levels and if you don't specify a value at one level, Kitto x tries to synthesize a sensible default by inspecting higher levels. For example, if you don't specify a DisplayLabel for a field in a View, the DisplayLabel for the underlying model field is used, and if the specification is missing there as well, a label is created by beautifying the field name.

This means that in Kitto x you generally only specify variations from the common standard way, and that if you use sensible conventions you are going

title: Business Rules
summary: A rule in Kitto x is a business rule, or constraint, applied during data entry. Rules are the heart of any non-trivial application: they are where the business logic lives, declaratively attached to the data model rather than scattered across the user interface.
keywords: How rules are attached to models
text:
Business Rules 

A rule in Kitto x is a business rule, or constraint, applied during data entry. Rules are the heart of any non-trivial application: they are where the business logic lives, declaratively attached to the data model rather than scattered across the user interface.

A rule can:

 validate data and block the operation with an error message (e.g. "Codice Fiscale already exists");
 compute / set field values (defaults, descriptions, totals, cascaded values from a referenced record);
 react to a field change (look up related data, recalculate dependent fields, show/hide editors);
 enforce cross-field or cross-record integrity before writing to the database.

Because rules are declared in the model (and optionally refined in the view), the same business logic is enforced consistently everywhere that model is edited — every List, every Form, every master-detail, regardless of which controller triggered the operation. This is the Kitto x way of applying Don't Repeat Yourself to business logic.

 How rules are attached to models

A rule is attached by adding a subnode to the object you want to constrain, and listing the rule by name (with optional parameters) underneath it. You can attach rules at four levels:

 Level | Where | When applied |
 
 Model | at the top of a file | Always, whenever a record of that model is created, edited or deleted. |
 Model field | under a field in | Always, unless a view-table-field rule of the same type overrides it. |
 View table | under a / detail table in a file | Only when editing through that view, in addition to (and before) the model rules. |
 View table field | under a field in a view | Only when editing through that view; overrides the model-field rule of the same type. |

The override mechanism follows convention over configuration: a field-level rule defined in the model is the default, and a view can replace it for a specific screen (for example force upper case in the model, but a different behaviour in one special form).

Here is the model-level attachment, taken from the real model of the KittoSCM sample application:

Notes from the example above:

 Several rules can be stacked on the same field; they fire in declaration order.
 is a predefined rule, the others are custom rules written in Delphi for this application.
 passes a value to the rule (a template expanded with the record's fields). Rules can also take named sub-parameters (see Rule parameters).
 Rules on a field ( ) typically run when the user picks a value in the lookup and cascade data into other fields.

 The rule lifecycle

Every rule is a Delphi class descending from (unit ). You implement a rule by overriding one or more of the methods that Kitto x calls at well-defined moments of the editing lifecycle. The default implementation of every method does nothing, so you only override what you need.

 Method | Called when | Typical use |
 
 | A new record is created, before it is shown | Set computed default values (declarative is already applied). |
 | An existing record is opened for editing | Block editing of locked records; set transient values. |
 | After the edit form has been built | Show/hide or enable editors based on the record. |
 | A record is being duplicated | Reset or adjust values that must not be copied. |
 | Before a field value changes | Disallow the change ( ), or rewrite . |
 | After a field value changed | Look up related data, recalculate dependent fields, validate the single value. |
 | After a reference field is refreshed | Update editors that depend on the referenced record. |
 | Server-side, before INSERT (for detail rows: when the row enters the master's in-memory store) | Cross-field validation specific to new records. A rejected detail row is removed from the store. |
 | Server-side, before UPDATE (for detail rows: when the edited row is written to the in-memory store) | Cross-field validation specific to updates. A rejected detail row gets its previous values back. |

text:
CalendarPanel 

 tip Kitto x Enterprise feature
The CalendarPanel is part of the Kittoˣ Enterprise edition. See the Feature Matrix for the full comparison with the Open-Source edition.

The CalendarPanel is a data panel controller that renders an interactive calendar using EventCalendar. It displays a ViewTable's records as events on a calendar with month, week, and day views.

The CalendarPanel is typically used as a inside a List controller, following the same pattern as ChartPanel. The calendar auto-fetches events from the server based on the visible date range.

 Basic usage 

The node contains the field mappings that tell the calendar which model fields to use for the event ID, start/end dates, title, type (for color-coding), and notes.

 Field mapping 

Field mappings are defined under the node. All mappings are optional — sensible defaults are used when a mapping is not specified:

 Property | Default | Description |
 
 | First key field of the model | Field containing the unique event identifier |
 | | Field containing the event start date/time |
 | | Field containing the event end date/time. If omitted, or when it maps to the same field as , events are treated as point-in-time and drawn with the duration |
 | | Field displayed as the event title in the calendar |
 | | Field used for automatic color grouping (optional) |
 | | Field displayed as a secondary line below the title in the week and day views (optional, auto-detected) |

If is not explicitly mapped, the controller looks for a field named in the model. If no such field exists, notes are simply not shown.

 Calendar options 

Calendar display options are set in the node:

 Property | Default | Description |
 
 | | Initial calendar view: , , or |
 | | Earliest time displayed in week/day views (e.g., to hide night hours) |
 | | Latest time displayed in week/day views (e.g., ) |
 | | Duration, in minutes, given to events that have no end date or whose end is not after the start (for example a record with a single date/time). Without it such events would be drawn as a zero-height strip in the week and day views |
 | | HTML template file (from ) used to render event content inside calendar cells. The template can use field placeholders to display custom event details |

Example with custom options:

 Event content 

What an event shows depends on the view:

 Month view ( ): one line per event, with the start time followed by the title.
 Week and day views ( , ): the block's position already tells the time, so the event shows the title and, below it, the notes field mapped by (for example an address or a description).

An replaces this default rendering in every view.

 Event colors 

When a field is mapped (or an field exists in the model), each distinct value receives a color from a built-in palette of 10 colors. Colors are assigned automatically in order of first appearance — no manual color configuration is required.

The palette provides visually distinct colors that work well on both light and dark themes.

 Event selection and CRUD 

The CalendarPanel supports the same CRUD operations as List, with a toolbar containing Add, Edit, Delete, and View buttons. Button visibility and permissions follow the standard action rules ( , ).

 Event interaction follows the same pattern as grid row selection:

 Single click on an event selects it (visual highlight) and enables the Edit/Delete/View toolbar buttons.
 Double click on an event opens the Edit form (or View form if editing is not allowed).
 Click on an empty cell opens the Add form.
 Toolbar buttons work on the currently selected event.

After a form save or delete, the calendar refreshes automatically and the selection is cleared.

 Edit form 

The calendar uses the same Form controller as List views. Configure the form layout via :

All options (Width, Height, CloneButton, layout nodes, etc.) work exactly as they do in List views.

text:
How to style applications by means of CSS 

 Kitto x uses a CSS custom properties (variables) system defined in . All UI components reference these variables, making it easy to customize the look and feel globally.

 Themes 

 Kitto x supports Light, Dark and Auto themes out of the box. The node in Config.yaml carries , shared / / / , and per-mode / sub-nodes (each with its own ):

See the Themes page for the full reference and real-world examples.

This page focuses on the next step: overriding individual CSS rules and custom properties when the built-in options are not enough.

 CSS Custom Properties 

The main variables you can override to customize the appearance include:

 Variable | Description |
 
 | Page background color |
 | Surface color (panels, cards) |
 | Primary text color |
 | Accent color for active elements |
 | Toolbar and button background |
 | Toolbar and button text color |
 | Border color |
 | Form input border color |
 | Error/danger color |

 Custom CSS 

You can customize individual CSS styles by adding code to your file, which is included in every Kitto x application by default. For example:

To inspect the structure and naming of Kitto x CSS classes, use your browser's developer tools (F12).

 Theme-adaptive backgrounds ( + ) {theme-adaptive-backgrounds}

Fixed hex backgrounds — even pleasant pastels like or — break when the user switches to dark mode: the page text becomes light ( from in dark) and ends up unreadable on a light pastel. Instead of writing two separate rules for and , mix your accent against so the background inherits the active theme's surface and the contrast against stays predictable in both palettes:

 In light mode is → the mix produces the same pastel you would have written by hand (gold, rose).
 In dark mode is → the mix produces a deep burnt-gold or muted red, with the lighter still readable.

The same idea applies wherever you would otherwise hardcode a colour: avoid in HtmlPanel HTML; use (or when on a chrome surface) and the styling follows the theme without per-mode duplication.

 SVG Icon System 

 Kitto x uses Material Design Icons rendered via CSS . Icons are referenced by name through the property in YAML metadata (e.g., ). Five styles are available ( , , , , ), configurable via in Config.yaml. Icon sizes ( 1em, 1.4em, 1.8em) are configurable via . See the icon name mapping in ( ) for the full list of available icons.

title: ChangePassword Controller
summary: By default opens a windows that allows the user to change the password.
keywords: Authenticators that do not support the change
text:
ChangePassword Controller 

By default opens a windows that allows the user to change the password.

For example, you can use the controller in a MainMenu file as following:

and this is the result:

 Voluntary change and imposed change 

The same controller serves two different situations, and it adapts itself to them.

 Situation | Old Password field | Server-side check |
 
 The user picks Change Password from the menu | shown and required | the old password must match the stored one |
 The change is imposed ( ) | not shown | skipped |

The change is imposed after a registration or a password reset, when the user has
received a temporary password by mail — or after an administrator forced a reset. In
that case asking for the old password would be asking for something the user never
chose, so the field is not rendered at all, is not submitted, and the check is
skipped on the server too.

 comes from the authenticator: the base implementation reads the
 item of the session authentication data, which the 
authenticator fills from the columns returned by its query. When
it is True the framework shows this view as the home page, and the user cannot reach
the application until the password has been changed — and that is enforced on
every request, not only on the home page: while the flag is set, endpoints outside this view
answer . This requires the view to be named exactly ; see
Imposed steps are enforced server-side. See
ConfigAuth for the authenticator configuration.

 Password verification 

The controller never compares password hashes on its own: both the old-password check
and the "new password must differ from the current one" check go through the
authenticator's method, which each authenticator may implement its
own way. The authenticator, for one, stores a salted bcrypt value that
cannot be recomputed from the clear password: only its own verifier can tell whether
the two match, so a literal comparison of hashes would always fail.

For the same reason, when the authenticator reports , the clear-text
password is handed to it instead of an MD5 hash: computing the hash up front would
produce a value the verifier could never match.

 Authenticators that do not support the change 

Not every authenticator can change a password, and the dialog now asks before letting
the user type one: is checked when the view is displayed and again
by the endpoint. Where it answers the user gets an explicit
message and nothing is written:

 Authenticator | Change | Why |
 
 , , | yes | they own the stored credential |
 | no | passwords live in the directory |
 | no | the user list file is not rewritten by the application |
 | no | the accounts are database-server users — a DBA job |
 | no | there is no account |

A JWT envelope does not affect this table: password change depends on the underlying authenticator (the rows above), and the token layer is orthogonal to it.

 tip
For a configuration whose authenticator cannot change passwords, keeping this view out of the
menu is tidier than showing a menu item that always refuses.

 When no password is stored 

The "new password must differ from the current one" check is skipped when the session
carries no stored password, because there is nothing to differ from. That covers two
cases that would otherwise be stuck:

 an account created without a password — an administrator adding a user from a form that
 has no password field, for instance. Note that such an account cannot be
 logged into (see No login with an empty password),
 so it is reached through the password-reset flow, which sets a temporary password and brings
 the user straight here;
 the OSDB authenticator using the system user name, which reports every password as
 matching because the operating system has already authenticated the user, and keeps no
 hash of its own.

 Password strength 

Strength rules are enforced by the authenticator, not by this controller: the new
password reaches , and it is that method that may reject it. The

text:
ChartPanel 

 tip Kitto x Enterprise feature
The ChartPanel is part of the Kittoˣ Enterprise edition. See the Feature Matrix for the full comparison with the Open-Source edition.

The ChartPanel is a data presenter that renders interactive charts using Chart.js. It displays a ViewTable's records as a chart; a data grid can sit beside it in a region of the hosting List.

The ChartPanel is typically used as a inside a List controller, which provides filtering capability and hosts the grid sidebar as a real GridPanel in its West or East region. The chart refreshes automatically when filters change and when the grid is refreshed.

The available chart types are: Bar, Line, Pie, and Doughnut. Bar and Line are cartesian charts (with X and Y axes), while Pie and Doughnut display slices proportional to data values.

 Cartesian charts (Bar, Line) 

Cartesian charts map a category field to one axis and a numeric field to the other. The chart type is determined by the value.

 Bar chart example 

The places a data grid to the left of the chart, showing the same data in tabular form, with the standard grid toolbar (sortable columns, Refresh). text:
The config file 

It is called Config.yaml by default, and it is the one mandatory file in a Kitto x application. Think of it as the main entry point. Normally the config file mentions a HomeView from which the entire application is served. The config file contains settings regarding database connections, language and localization, user authentication, access control and so on.

 warning Write comments on their own line
A starts a comment only at the beginning of a line. Everything that follows the colon is the value, up to the end of the line, so a trailing comment becomes part of the value: raises a conversion error on a boolean node, and is silently discarded in favour of the default. This applies to every YAML file of an application — Config, models, views and layouts.

List of first-level config nodes (click on node names for details):

 Name | Type | Description |
 
 AppTitle | String | Application title |
 Databases | Subnode | Database connections |
 Auth | Subnode | User authentication settings |
 AccessControl | Subnode | Access control (user privileges) settings |
 HomeTinyView HomeSmallView HomeView | String/Subnode | Specifies the view to display at application startup (or after login if user authentication is enabled) for client devices up to 5", from 6" to 10" and over 10" respectively |
 Theme | Subnode | Theme settings: ( , , ) plus optional sub-nodes for Primary-Color, Font-Family, Font-Size, IconStyle, IconSize |
 Log | Subnode | Logging-related settings |
 LanguageId | String | Default user interface language (such as en) |
 Charset | String | Default charset (normally utf-8) |
 FOPEnginePath | String | Default FOP Engine Path |
 JavaScriptLibraries | List | Optional libreries to include |
 Defaults | Subnode | Default settings for layout, grid, form panel, window |
 UserFormats | Subnode | User-facing formats: date, time, currency, decimal/thousand separators |
 Desktop | Subnode | Window properties for Desktop Embedded Mode (ClientWidth, ClientHeight, Maximized, Resizable, BorderIcons, Position) |
 Email | Subnode | Default email settings

A Config.yaml example from HelloKitto:

 UserFormats 

The node controls how dates, times, and numeric values are displayed throughout the application (both in grids and forms).

 Property | Type | Default | Description |
 
 | String | System default | Date display format (e.g. , ) |
 | String | System default | Time display format (e.g. , ) |
 | String | System default | Currency symbol displayed in currency fields (e.g. , , ) |
 | String | System default | Decimal separator character (e.g. for Italian, for US/UK) |
 | String | System default | Thousands separator character (e.g. for Italian, for US/UK) |

These settings override the system's default at application startup. This ensures consistent formatting across the entire application, regardless of the server's locale.

Currency fields in grids display the currency symbol before the formatted value (e.g. ). In forms, the currency symbol appears inside the input field and is temporarily removed while editing.

title: Access Control
summary: Access control is used in Kitto x to manage user access to resources. Resources in this context are everything that the user can access in any way, such as models, views and fields. Each resource is uniquely identified by a string in URI format, and supports one or more access modes.
keywords: Users, Roles and the Permissions Table
Server-side ACL enforcement on route handlers
text:
Access Control 

Access control is used in Kitto x to manage user access to resources. Resources in this context are everything that the user can access in any way, such as models, views and fields. Each resource is uniquely identified by a string in URI format, and supports one or more access modes.

A complete worked example with three roles ( / / ), six grant rows and a layered design that covers menu visibility, CRUD, field-level READ and Users-table protection ships with TasKitto — read this page first for the conceptual model, then jump there for the data you can copy-paste into your own app.

 Resources, Privileges and Access Modes 

A user can perform a given operation (access mode) on an object (resource) if she has the corresponding privilege(s). For example, in order to be able to change a field's value, you need to own the MODIFY privilege on both the ModelField and the ViewField that represents it. Plus, you need the MODIFY (if editing an existing record) or ADD (if creating a new record) privileges on the ViewTable and Model.

The following tables summarize the current built-in AC-enabled resource types in Kitto x and the access modes each of them supports. Since resource URIs and access modes are nothing but strings, you can add your own resource types and modes if you want, and hook them to the system

 Resource Type: Model

 Sample URI: 

 Access Mode | Meaning |
 
 READ | User can see the data |
 ADD | User can add new records |
 MODIFY | User can modify existing records |
 DELETE | User can delete records |

 Resource Type: ModelField

 Sample URI: 

 Access Mode | Meaning |
 
 READ | User can see the data (otherwise the particular field/column is not visible) |
 MODIFY | When editing or adding records, user can set the field's value |

When you don't grant MODIFY access to particular fields to a user that can add records, you must make sure that these fields, which will be read-only for the user, receive suitable default or otherwise computed values.

 Resource Type: View
 Sample URI: 

 Access Mode | Meaning |
 
 VIEW | User sees the view (in a menu or toolbar, for example) |
 RUN | User can launch the view by clicking it (otherwise the item will look disabled) |

If you want a user to see a feature that is not available to him, then you grant the VIEW mode but not the RUN mode to the relevant view.
If you want to completely hide a feature, you grant neither of them.

 Resource Type: ViewTable (part of a DataView)

 Sample URI: 

 Access Mode | Meaning |
 
 READ | User can see the data |
 ADD | User can add new records |
 MODIFY | User can modify existing records |
 DELETE | User can delete records |

Please note that a DataView's MainTable shares the same URI as the view. IOW, you don't need to individually grant privileges for a DataView and its MainTable.

You need to grant privileges both at the view and model level for them to be effective. This is so to allow you to make different views for different kinds of users based on the same models.

 Resource Type: ViewField (a field in a ViewTable)

 Sample URI: 

 Access Mode | Meaning |
 
 READ | User can see the data (otherwise the particular field/column is not visible) |
 MODIFY | When editing or adding records, user can set the field's value |

 Access Controllers 

Access control is implemented by a class that you can optionally enable. By default, the Null access controller class is used, which always grants access to everything. You can use a predefined access controller or create your own.

In order to enable an access controller you need to:

 Specify its name and settings in the config file.
 Include/use the relevant unit in your project.

 Kitto x ships two access controllers (besides the default Null one):

 Name | Unit | Description |
 
 DB | Kitto.AccessControl.DB | RBAC implementation reading and from a database. Hits the DB on first access per user/process and caches the result in memory for the session. |
 JWT | Kitto.AccessControl.JWT |

summary: User authentication in Kitto x is optional. If an application needs to authenticate users, an authenticator among a selection of predefined ones can be enabled, or a custom authentication can be developed.

text:
User authentication 

User authentication in Kitto x is optional. If an application needs to authenticate users, an authenticator among a selection of predefined ones can be enabled, or a custom authentication can be developed.

In order to enable an authenticator you need to:

 Specify its name and settings in the config file.
 Include/use the relevant unit in your project.

Standard authenticators ( parameter values):

 Name | Unit | Description |
 
 DB | Kitto.Auth.DB | Uses a database table of users and optionally hashed passwords |
 DBCrypt | Kitto.Auth.DB | Same user table as , but passwords are bcrypt-hashed in the column. |
 DBServer | Kitto.Auth.DBServer | Authenticates users as DB server users. Requires a block that reads the typed credentials through the macros — see Auth: DBServer. |
 OSDB | Kitto.Auth.OSDB | Uses Operating System authentication |
 TextFile | Kitto.Auth.TextFile | Uses a text file of users and optionally hashed passwords. See Auth: TextFile. |
 LDAP | Kitto.Auth.LDAP | Validates users with a simple bind against an LDAP directory (Active Directory or generic LDAP); no local user table. See Auth: LDAP. |
The JWT envelope is not an authenticator of its own: it is an optional sub-block you add under any of the authenticators above (unit ), which issues a self-contained signed JWT in an HttpOnly cookie that replaces the opaque session id. See JWT envelope for the full reference.

Other authentication methods will be added. Plus, it's easy to tweak existing authenticators and create inherited modified versions.

By default, the Null authenticator is used, which does not require user authentication. It
accepts every request as an authenticated anonymous session, and refuses password change, password
reset and PIN/QR enrolment: there is no account for it to write to.

 Startup checks

Two configuration mistakes stop the application at startup, with the reason in the log:

 Configuration | What happens |
 
 names a class that nobody registered — a typo, or the unit missing from | The application refuses to start, and the message lists the class ids actually registered. Only is registered by the core: , , , , and each need their unit in the project's . ( is not an authenticator class — it is an optional envelope added under one of these.) |
 whose block has fixed credentials | The application refuses to start. This authenticator validates a login by opening the connection with the supplied credentials, so a with its own user name and password checks nothing and accepts everyone. See Auth: DBServer. |

 The Login dialog 

When authentication is enabled, a Kitto x application displays a Login dialog at startup, unless all required credentials are specified by other means.

Credentials can vary depending on the authenticator, but usually they are UserName and Password, both of type String.

The other available means of specifying credentials, needed in special cases, are basically two:

 In the Config file, inside a Auth/Defaults subnode.
 In the URL, as standard URL parameters.

 warning What credentials in the URL do, and do not, do

resolved and the home renders. But it does not go through the endpoint, so no token
is issued: with a JWT envelope no token cookie is set, and under
 there is no claim, which is closed-world. The result is a home page
where every view is denied and only Logout is visible — an apparently broken session rather than
a working login. F5 also repeats the credentials, so the login page never returns.

The credentials are also exposed where a URL goes: the address bar, the browser history, and the
 header sent to any external link on the page. They do not reach the log, which
records the path without the query string.

Use it for what it is meant for — a deliberate deep link, a kiosk, an integration — and prefer
 when the goal is simply to pre-fill or preset credentials. The
application itself never produces such a URL: se

title: JWT envelope
summary: A sub-block under any authenticator turns on a self-contained signed JSON Web Token, issued in an HttpOnly cookie on a successful login and validated on every subsequent request. The token replaces the legacy opaque session-id cookie and carries selected user-profile claims ( , , , , ).
keywords: Cookies emitted with a JWT envelope
text:
JWT envelope

A sub-block under any authenticator turns on a self-contained signed JSON Web Token, issued in an HttpOnly cookie on a successful login and validated on every subsequent request. The token replaces the legacy opaque session-id cookie and carries selected user-profile claims ( , , , , ).

The JWT envelope is orthogonal to the authenticator: the credential check stays with whatever you configured ( , , , , a custom class…), and the block just adds the token layer on top. Presence of the node is what enables it — remove the block and the same authenticator falls back to a plain server-side session cookie.

It is opt-in and additive: an application on / / a custom authenticator with no block is untouched and does not pull in the underlying delphi-jose-jwt library. To use JWT, add to the clause of (see Opt-in) and add the JOSE source folder to the unit search path. That unit provides the JOSE-backed engine and registers it at startup; the core stays JOSE-free.

 When to use it

 You want stateless authentication that survives multiple instances behind a load balancer.
 You need a verified credential carried on every request without a server-side lookup.
 You want to embed the user profile (display name, environment, language, roles) in the credential itself.
 You plan to integrate external identity providers (OIDC, SAML) — the JWT envelope is the architectural extension point for those (see Extension points).

 Opt-in from UseKitto.pas

Add to your application's . The unit registers the JOSE-backed JWT engine (via in its ), so the base can issue and validate tokens whenever an block is present. Register a key provider in the same block so all flavors of your app (Standalone, ISAPI, Desktop, Apache module) share the same signing key without each having to set an environment variable:

The argument is matched (case-insensitive) against , so the same provider is used across all flavors of the app while leaving other JWT-enabled apps in the same process free to register their own key. The registered provider always takes precedence over in .

Then add the JOSE source folder to the unit search path:

 warning If the engine is not linked
If a contains an block but is missing from , no engine is registered and the first token operation raises an explanatory error ("add Kitto.Auth.JWT to your project's UseKitto.pas"). The core deliberately carries no JOSE dependency, so it cannot issue tokens on its own.

 Minimal configuration

If no provider is registered in , is read from the YAML — set the environment variable (or use or an literal) before starting the server.

 Full configuration reference

The authenticator's own keys (credential check, storage, login-form behaviour) stay directly under , exactly as they are without a token. Only the token envelope keys go under .

 How it works at runtime

The orchestration lives in the base ; the JOSE crypto lives in the engine ( , in the opt-in ). is simply "is there an node?" — every step below is a no-op when it is .

1. Login ( ) — the authenticator performs its normal credential check. On success calls , which delegates to the engine: it builds the claim set, signs it with the configured algorithm and key, and writes the compact form into the cookie.
2. Subsequent requests — decodes the JWT payload (base64url + JSON, without verifying the signature) to recover the claim and bind the request to its server-side . The decode is purely for routing; it grants no privilege, and the engine detects a JWT app by the presence of the node, not by a class check — so apps that don't use JWT pay for no JOSE dependency.
3. Auth gate — right after , the request filter calls the polymorphic . When , the base delegates to the engine to validate the JWT signature plus the , , , and claims. If the token is invalid the cookie is cleared and is set to (the user is redirected to the login page on the next protected route).  tip Edit connections visually
KIDE x 's Config Editor has a dedicated Databases panel that edits these connections visually and validates them with a Test Connection button before you run the app. The New Project Wizard also adds the matching data-access driver units to based on the drivers you select.

A single Kitto x application can work on multiple databases, of different kinds. The node in contains one or more subnodes, each containing the connection params to a database. The subnode called is the one used by default for database access.
Give a different name to each subnode as in the following example:

 Adapters 

An adapter is a wrapper that allows Kitto x to connect to a particular database (or a family of databases) through a particular data access library. Currently Kitto x has four adapters:
 DBX to use Delphi's DBExpress data access layer.
 ADO to use Microsoft's ADO.
 FD to use Delphi's FireDac data access layer.
 ODAC to use Devart's Oracle Data Access Components — Oracle only, optional (requires an ODAC license; see Oracle via Devart ODAC below).

More adapters can be developed and plugged in as needed.

The adapter is specified by name as the value of each database's subnode.

 Database types 

Each adapter detects the type of database it is using and uses this information to affect the behaviour of Kitto x , for example to generate slightly different SQL statements depending on the particular dialect the database understands.

 Delimited identifiers ( ) 

By default Kitto x emits table and column names as-is in the SQL it generates. This works for the usual identifiers, but fails when a table or column name contains spaces (or other characters that are illegal in a bare SQL identifier) — typical of legacy / imported databases such as Northwind ( , , …). The result is a syntax error like "Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'of'".

Set on a database subnode (sibling of ) to make the SQL builder wrap every identifier in the delimiters of that database's dialect:

The flag is opt-in and per-database (default ): databases without it keep the exact previous behaviour. The delimiter is chosen automatically from the dialect:

 Database | Delimiter | Example |
 
 SQL Server | | |
 PostgreSQL / Firebird / Oracle / ANSI | | |
 MySQL / MariaDB | | |

Multi-part names are split on the dot and each part is delimited separately, so a schema/catalog prefix is handled correctly: → (never ).

 Prerequisites and limitations

 Exact case required (PostgreSQL / Oracle / Firebird). Delimiting with makes identifiers case-sensitive: is not the same object as . When is on, the of each Model/field must match the spelling stored in the database exactly. (On SQL Server, does not change case sensitivity, which follows the collation.)
 Free SQL is never delimited. Anything you author yourself — field , , , , filter-panel / , and macros — is emitted verbatim. If such an expression references an identifier with spaces, you delimit it yourself in the YAML (for example ).
 Parameter names. The fix delimits identifiers in the generated SQL; query parameter names are unaffected.

 Connection subnode

PostgreSQL groups database objects into schemas (the equivalent of SQL Server schemas, not databases). When the SQL refers to an unqualified table (for example rather than ), PostgreSQL resolves the name through the session-level .

Logging 

You can enable server side logging in Kitto x , which will allow you to see trace data useful for debugging or log your own data from your server side code (such as custom controllers or rules, for example). The logging system is pluggable and multiple loggers can be active at once.

 Logging to file 

In order to enable logging to file, you write something like this in your Config.yaml:

The code above uses the logger, which you also need to enable in your application by referencing the unit (usually in your file). If you fail to include the relevant unit, your logging configuration will be ineffective.

 Log levels 

The parameter controls the verbosity of log output:

 Level | Description |
 
 | Minimal — errors and critical events only |
 | Warnings |
 | Informational messages |
 | Verbose |
 | Debug — full trace output |

 warning
 generates huge amounts of data; use it only while debugging.

 Available loggers 

 Logger | Unit | Config section | Description |
 
 TextFile | | | Writes to a plain text file |
 CodeSite | | | Sends log data to the CodeSite viewer (any edition) |

Each logger section must contain at least . You can disable a logger without removing its configuration by setting . To log to file and CodeSite at the same time, just add both sections under the node.

 Passwords in the log 

Credentials never reach the log: before a message is written, the value assigned to anything whose name contains password is replaced with . All the shapes a message can carry one in are covered — from a query string, from JSON, from a SQL trace.

The message itself is kept. A line that merely mentions the word — a marker, an error such as Old Password is wrong, the name of a method — is logged unchanged, so authentication stays diagnosable.

 tip Why this matters when you are debugging
Earlier versions dropped the whole line whenever it contained the word. Anything you added to trace an authentication problem disappeared silently, which made the execution look as if it stopped between two consecutive statements. If you are reading logs written by an older build, keep that in mind.

 Saving errors 

When a save fails, the message shown in the browser is also written to the log, prefixed with and carrying the exception class. You therefore have a record of the failure once the dialog has been closed, and something to look at when a user reports the problem second-hand.

It is logged at level , so it appears whenever is or above — you do not have to turn the log up to to see it.

 Unhandled request exceptions 

An exception that escapes every handler while a request is being served is logged at level 
as , next to the modal dialog the browser gets.

 tip Why this matters
The modal dialog is not the only trace of an escaped exception — it is also logged. Without that
log line a Windows service, an ISAPI module or an Apache module, none of which shows the dialog,
would leave no record at all, and a diagnosis that started from "the log shows nothing between these
two statements" would be reading a log that could not show it.

 Why a login was refused 

Every refusal that is not simply a wrong password says so in the log, so a support call does
not turn into guesswork. Nothing here prints a credential — see Passwords in the log.

 | 3 | The account exists but its password column is empty or NULL: it cannot be logged into. Send a temporary password with the reset flow |

 | 3 | without a per-user secret, see PIN login |
 | 3 | Misconfiguration: with a value it is a master password, without one it would accept a blank password for everybody |
 | 4 | The imposed-step gate refused an endpoint outside the required view |
 | 4 | The authentication gate answered |

text:
Dashboard

 tip Kitto x Enterprise feature
The Dashboard controller is part of the Kittoˣ Enterprise edition. See the Feature Matrix for the full comparison with the Open-Source edition.

The Dashboard controller extends FlexPanel with a JavaScript-driven auto-refresh capability. It is designed to display KPI cards, charts, and summary views in a responsive grid layout that can automatically poll the server for updated data — patching the DOM in place, never recreating it.

The screenshot above shows the TasKitto Activity Dashboard with four KPI cards in the first row, two chart views in the second row, and a daily trend chart spanning the full width at the bottom.

 tip A Dashboard view declares no 
A Dashboard is a container: it draws the views listed under , and has no table of its
own. Its view still says , because that is what selects the data-view metadata class
and makes the controller a data controller — it is not a promise that a or a
 exists. The same holds for a ChartPanel and for tool panels.

The framework treats that shape as legitimate: the decorations of a table with no model (its
label, its image), its behaviour flags ( , / / ,
 , , ) and the access check all degrade quietly instead of
failing.

 Configuration

 Dashboard-specific properties

 Property | Default | Description |
 
 | | Auto-refresh interval in seconds. = disabled. When enabled, the dashboard is updated incrementally in place: KPI text values are patched and chart data is applied via without recreating canvases |

All other properties are inherited from FlexPanel: , , , , , , and .

 Fixed heights for chart items

When a dashboard contains ChartPanel items, each item must specify a fixed in pixels. Without an explicit height, Chart.js cannot determine the canvas size and the charts will render incorrectly.

KPI cards based on TemplateDataPanel should also have a fixed height for visual consistency:

 Auto-refresh mechanism

When is greater than 0, the controller emits an inline script that activates the framework's poller (defined in ):

On each tick, the poller performs two silent fetches in sequence and applies their results in place:

1. KPI tiles — fetches the dashboard view HTML, parses it with , and replaces only the of every element whose value differs from the live one. Cards, headers, icons and footers are never touched.
2. Charts — for each inside the dashboard, fetches the JSON endpoint and applies it via . The Chart.js instance is reused; canvases are never destroyed and recreated.

Both steps short-circuit when their payload hashes match the previous tick (no DOM write when nothing changed). The fetches are serialized to avoid races against the framework's view-metadata access from concurrent worker threads. The poller pauses while is true (Page Visibility API) and stops automatically when the dashboard container leaves the DOM (e.g. tab closed).

The result is a dashboard that updates without flicker, without flashing the global loading overlay, and without the visual reset of charts on every refresh.

 kxDashboard JS API

 must be the dashboard's and the script tag is emitted automatically by the framework — manual calls are needed only when embedding a dashboard outside the standard tab-pane flow.

 tip
Set during development and enable it only in production to avoid unnecessary server load.

text:
DataPanelLeaf 

The data panel controllers are the ones that display record data linked to a ViewTable (see DataView). They share one abstract base class, , and split in two families, as in Kitto1:

 the host ( ): the List. It owns the list of data (filter panel, action flags, lookup context) and composes the presenters that show it in its regions.
 the presenters, or leaves ( ): each shows the same data in one way. A presenter works on its own at the root of a view (a with its own filters and toolbar) or hosted in a region of a List, in which case it takes the filter expression, the actions and the list-level options from the host.

You never use the base classes directly — you use one of the concrete controllers.

 Class hierarchy 

As a Panel, every data panel inherits the common panel properties ( , , , , , , , etc.) and the border regions ( , , ...).

 The controllers 

 Controller | Role | Description |
 
 List | host | Filters, actions and regions; the grid in its Center by default |
 GridPanel | presenter | Tabular data grid with sorting, column layouts, row colors |
 GroupingList | presenter | A GridPanel with collapsible group headers |
 TemplateDataPanel | presenter | Custom HTML templates for read-only display |
 ChartPanel | presenter | Chart.js charts (bar, line, pie, doughnut) |
 CalendarPanel | presenter | Events on a month/week/day calendar |
 Form | presenter | The current record, in a dialog or hosted beside the grid |

 Common features 

All data panels share these capabilities:

 ToolViews 

Custom action buttons on the controller's toolbar. Each ToolView launches a Tool controller:

 controls whether the button requires a selected row ( ) or is always enabled ( ).

 Standard actions 

Data panels support the standard CRUD operations Add, Duplicate, Edit, Delete, View, Refresh. Which of them a presenter offers is decided by the host from its flags ( , , ... at the level or under ), the view table's read-only state and the user's permissions; a presenter then narrows them to what it can show (a chart has no actions, a calendar has no Duplicate). See Standard actions.

The toolbar buttons appear in this order: Add, Duplicate, Edit, Delete, View, Refresh, then any custom ToolViews.

 AutoOpen and PagingTools 

 Property | Type | Default | Description |
 
 | Boolean | | Auto-load the data when the view opens. When , the grid opens empty until the user applies a filter or clicks Refresh. |
 | Boolean | | Show the pager bar (server-side pagination). Grid only. |

Both live under ; see AutoOpen and PagingTools.

Defines the initial sort order for the data panel:

Multiple fields can be specified separated by spaces (e.g. ).

 DefaultFilter 

A SQL clause applied automatically to restrict displayed records. Supports macros:

title: Data Based Views
summary: The DataView (a view with ) is a special kind of view that is data-bound. In a data-driven Kitto x application, it's the most common type of view.
text:
Data Based Views 

The DataView (a view with ) is a special kind of view that is data-bound. In a data-driven Kitto x application, it's the most common type of view.

Data in kitto applications is conveyed through Models. You might want to have a look at what a model is and how model relationships work before going on with data views.

 tip Generate DataViews from a Model
The DataView Wizard in KIDE x generates the complete / / structure described below from a Model, including a default filter. This page documents the YAML it produces, which you can then refine in the View & Layout Editor.

 Data views and controllers 

A data view can currently use two kinds of controllers:
 List displays a list of records in a grid that can be paginated, filtered and grouped.
 Form displays a form for viewing or editing a single record, using a customizable field layout.
 Chart displays a Chart. You may define the kind of chart (Pie Chart, Bar Chart, ..) using the node. 

Other controllers for data views are being designed and developed.

These controllers share some properties, which are specified under the Controller subnode of the data view and its data tables.

 Structure of a data view 

A data view embeds a , which is a view table object. The main table may have a set of detail tables (also view table objects), each of which may have a set of subdetail tables, and so on, forming a tree of data, depending on the relationships among models. A view table has an underlying , and represents a set of record fetched according to the model specification. By default, this means all the existing records, but they can be limited in various ways: fixed criteria, access-control filters, user filters, master/detail relationships. A view table has a set of view fields, which are view-level equivalents of model fields. You can override just about any model or model field property at the view table or view field level.

in the above example is the underlying Model.

Among the typical properties of a view table:

 : Overrides the model's DisplayLabel. Used as a label when displaying a single record. If missing, it is synthesized.
 : Overrides the model's PluralDisplayLabel. Used as a label when displaying multiple records. If missing, the singular display label is "pluralized".
 : Overrides the model's read-only state. Determines whether to display update tools (new/edit/delete) or not.
 : Overrides the model's Fields node. List of model fields to display. Fields from referenced models can be included in the form . Each subnode has the field name as its name and optionally the display label as the value. If you don't specify a display label, it is inherited from the underlying model field. You can override any model field property (such as , , , etc.) by adding subnodes under each view field. In the case of rules, the new rules are added rather than replaced. You cannot replace a model-level rule at the view level.

IIS loads the DLL and calls / for each request. WebBroker creates / pairs. delegates to , which owns a and calls . From this point on, the request pipeline is identical to the standalone server.

 Step 2: Prepare the deployment folders

 Kitto x uses a two-level directory structure on the server:

At runtime, the framework first looks for files in the Application Home; if not found, it falls back to the System Home. This means you deploy the framework once and share it across multiple applications.

FlexPanel

The FlexPanel is a container controller that arranges child views using CSS Flexbox layout. It renders all child views server-side (inline) rather than via parallel HTMX requests, avoiding thread-safety issues in the macro expansion engine.

Each child view is wrapped in a styled flex item with an optional title bar (from the view's ) and an optional footer (from YAML configuration).

 Configuration

 Container properties

 Property | Default | Description |

 Item properties

Items are defined under the node. Each item references a View by name.

 Property | Default | Description |
 
 | (required) | Name of the view to render in this flex item |

 | — | Text displayed in a footer bar below the item content |

The title bar is automatically generated from the child view's property. It is displayed at the top of each flex item with a styled background.

 MaxColumns layout

When is set, the flex-basis is calculated to ensure at most N items per row:

For example, with and :
 Each item gets a basis of ≈ 25% minus gaps
 Items wrap to the next row when more than 4 are present
 Individual items can still be wider if their value or forces it

 Child view rendering

FlexPanel renders child views inline on the server side. This means:

 All child views are rendered in a single HTTP response
 No parallel HTMX requests are generated for individual items
 Panel chrome (header, close button) is automatically suppressed on child views
 Any controller type can be used as a child: TemplateDataPanel, ChartPanel, List, Form, etc.
 If a child view fails to render, an error message is displayed in its flex item instead of breaking the entire layout

text:
Form Controller 

Displays a single record of a data view. It is usually called by a List controller when the user selects a record to view or edit, or creates a new record, but it can be used in stand-alone manner in special cases, such as insert-only forms, or editing data in single-record tables.

 Fields and editors 

The form controller renders a form panel with an editor for each field in the (main) view table; it can also show tabs or buttons for detail datasets. In read-write mode, it also features confirm and cancel buttons, whereas in read-only mode it has a close button only.

As mentioned above, each view table field generates an editor. The type of editor depends on the field's data type. For example, a date field features a popup date picker, a Boolean field a checkbox, a Reference field a combo box, a Currency field a text input with currency symbol formatting, and so on. Editor types are pluggable, so new editor types can be developed in Delphi.

Editor rendering is centralised in ( ), which is shared by both the Form controller and the List controller's filter panel. This ensures that the same field types produce consistent HTML elements and CSS classes regardless of context.

Editors are laid out vertically in the (scrollable) form panel, unless a layout definition is provided.

The GoogleMap controller is part of the Kittoˣ Enterprise edition. See the Feature Matrix for the full comparison with the Open-Source edition.

The GoogleMap controller renders an interactive Google Maps view with markers positioned via client-side geocoding of address fields from the database. It includes an optional data grid sidebar with a draggable splitter, similar to the ChartPanel layout.

The GoogleMap controller is a standalone data panel ( ) that reads model records, concatenates address fields for geocoding, and displays the results as map markers. Clicking a marker shows an InfoWindow with record details; clicking a grid row centers the map on the corresponding marker.

 Obtaining a Google Maps API Key 

The GoogleMap controller requires a Google Maps API key. To obtain one:

1. Go to the Google Cloud Console
2. Create a new project (or select an existing one)
3. Navigate to APIs & Services > Library
4. Enable the following APIs:
 - Maps JavaScript API — required to display the map
 - Geocoding API — required to convert addresses to coordinates
 - Directions API — only needed if using routing features
5. Navigate to APIs & Services > Credentials
6. Click Create Credentials > API Key
7. (Recommended) Restrict the key to your application's HTTP referrers

 warning API Key Security
The API key is embedded in the web page and visible to users. Always restrict it to specific HTTP referrers in the Google Cloud Console to prevent unauthorized use. Never use an unrestricted key in production.

Configure the key globally in :

Individual views can override the key via the node.

 Basic usage 

The controller geocodes each record's address (built by concatenating the fields listed in ) and places a marker on the map. The is displayed as the InfoWindow header, and the remaining (excluding the title field to avoid duplication) form the InfoWindow body.

title: GridPanel
summary: The GridPanel is the grid presenter: it shows the records of a view table as a paged, sortable table with a toolbar of standard actions. It is a DataPanelLeaf controller and as such inherits all its base class' capabilities, such as ToolViews.
text:
GridPanel 

The GridPanel is the grid presenter: it shows the records of a view table as a paged, sortable table with a toolbar of standard actions. It is a DataPanelLeaf controller and as such inherits all its base class' capabilities, such as ToolViews.

You rarely name it in YAML. It is what a List controller shows in its Center when no is declared, and what the Form controller uses to display detail records. You name it when you want a grid beside another presenter (TasKitto, ):

Hosted in a List, the grid takes from it what belongs to the list of data: the filter panel (rendered by the List above its content), the standard action flags and the lookup context. What follows describes what the grid itself draws. The grid may be either a plain grid or, through the GroupingList controller, a grouped grid with collapsible headers.

 Toolbar 

Above the table the grid renders its toolbar: Add, Duplicate, Edit, Delete, View, Refresh, the optional Help button, then the custom ToolViews declared under . Which standard buttons appear is decided by the hosting List (flags, read-only view table, user permissions). Buttons that act on a record are enabled once a row is selected.

 Double-click to open 

Double-clicking a row opens the record form:

 If the Edit action is visible and allowed for the current user, double-click opens the form in edit mode.
 Otherwise, if the View action is visible, double-click opens the form in view mode.
 If neither action is available, double-click has no effect.

The form opens as a dialog, or in the side panel when the List hosts the form of the current record. In a lookup dialog a double click picks the row instead. This behavior is automatic and applies to the GroupingList controller as well.

 Fields and columns 

The grid has a column for each field in the ViewTable it is linked to. The type of each column depends on the underlying field's data type.

You can add fields from referenced models through the dot syntax ( ), in which case you must also provide an alias to be used as field name ( ).

Example:

Column order equals the order of view table fields, unless a layout definition is provided.

 Cell tooltip on truncated content 

Cells have a fixed maximum width and truncate long text with an ellipsis ( ). When a cell is truncated, hovering it shows the full value as a native browser tooltip. The tooltip appears only when the text is actually clipped: if the column is wide enough to display the whole value, no tooltip is shown. Widening the column via the drag handle removes the tooltip once the content becomes fully visible; narrowing a column below the content width restores it. Boolean checkboxes and HTMLMemo cells are excluded (they contain non-textual content).

 Manual column resize 

Every column header has a thin drag handle on its right edge (visible on hover as an accent-colored strip). Click and drag horizontally to widen or narrow a single column while the other columns keep their autosized width. If the total width exceeds the visible area, a horizontal scrollbar appears at the bottom of the grid so the off-screen columns stay reachable.

While dragging, the cursor (the two-headed arrow with a vertical bar) is kept visible everywhere on the page, so it does not flip back to the regular pointer when the mouse passes over column titles or rows. A click generated at the end of the drag does not trigger a sort on the dragged column.

The resize is ephemeral: widths are not saved anywhere. Closing and re-opening the grid restores all columns to their autosized defaults.

 Column sorting 

Clicking a column header sorts the grid by that column. An arrow icon indicates the current sort direction:

 First click on a column: sorts ascending (↑ arrow)
 Click again on the same column: sorts descending (↓ arrow)
 Click a different column: sorts ascending by the new column (replaces previous sort)

The sort state persists across page navigation (when using PagingTools) and filter changes. Sorti

text:
GroupingList Controller 

The GroupingList controller renders a data grid with all records grouped by a specified field, featuring collapsible group headers with expand/collapse toggles. Unlike the standard List controller, GroupingList loads all records at once (no paging) and organizes them into visual groups.

It is a variant of the GridPanel presenter, reusing its toolbar, column headers and standard actions (Add, Edit, View, Delete), and it builds its own filter panel when it is the root controller of the view (or takes the filters of the hosting List). The only difference is in how records are displayed: instead of a flat paginated table, records appear under collapsible group headings.

 Basic usage 

Set on the view and configure the node under :

This produces a grid where activities are grouped by the TYPE field (resolved through its reference to display the type name), with each group initially collapsed. The group header shows the type name and the count of records, for example: Analysis (5 activities).

 Grouping configuration 

All grouping properties go under :

 Property | Type | Default | Description |
 
 | String | (required) | Name of the field to group by. Can be any field including reference fields (which display the referenced value) or expression-based fields. |
 | Boolean | | If , all groups appear initially collapsed (only the group header is visible). Users can click to expand. |
 | Boolean | | If , shows the record count in each group header. |
 | String | (empty) | Singular noun used when count is 1 (e.g. ). |
 | String | (empty) | Plural noun used when count > 1 (e.g. ). |
 | Boolean | | If , prefixes the group value with the field's display label (e.g. instead of just ). |
 | String | (grouping field) | Space-separated list of field names for the ORDER BY clause. Defaults to the grouping field. Use this to add a secondary sort within each group. |
 | Node | (none) | Per-group totals appended to each header — see Aggregates in the group header. |

 warning Properties inherited from Kitto1 metadata that are not supported
 and are accepted by the YAML parser but ignored.
See Migrating a grouped view from Kitto1.

 Aggregates in the group header 

Each child of names a field of the view table and describes what to compute over the records of the group:

 Property | Default | Description |
 
 | | , , , or . counts the non-null values of the field, which is not the same as the record count of . |
 | field's | Text shown before the value. Localized like every other label. |

Aggregates are listed in the order they appear in the YAML, each separated by , and they coexist with and .

 The value is formatted like the column it comes from: the user's format settings, and the currency symbol when the field is a . is always a plain integer.

 Only numeric fields can be aggregated. A field that does not exist in the view table, or that is not numeric, is skipped and the reason is written to the log — the header renders without it rather than failing. If a total you expect is missing, look there first.

 A group with nothing to report shows nothing. When the column is null throughout the group, the aggregate is left out instead of being rendered as zero, which would read as a real total. is the exception: zero is a legitimate answer to "how many values are there".

 tip Cost
Aggregates and share a single pass over the records, and that pass is skipped entirely when neither is declared. Adding aggregates to a view that already shows the count costs nothing.

 Group header format 

The group header text is built as follows:

 ShowName: False (default): 
 ShowName: True:

 ShowCount: True without ItemName/PluralItemName:

By default, records are sorted by the grouping field only. Use to define a multi-field sort:

This sorts first by TYPE (to keep groups together), then by ACTIVITYDATE within each group. Each

text:
Hello Kitto x 

HelloKitto is a sample application that you can use to explore the Kitto x way of doing things, understand the basic concepts behind the framework, get ideas and copy-paste snippets for your own experimentations.

To create your own application the recommended way is the New Project Wizard; copying and renaming an example directory like this one is a quick manual alternative.

 Languages 
HelloKitto is shipped translated in English, Italian, German, Spanish and Portuguese. The interface language follows the browser ( ) on the first visit and can be changed at any time with the flag LanguageSwitcher — on the login form and at the bottom of the left menu. See Localization for how the translation catalogs are built and maintained.

 Live Demo 
Click here to launch the Live Demo of HelloKitto — log in with UserName and Password .

Prefer to run it in your own environment? See Compiling and running the demos.

 Features 

The features of Kitto x used by HelloKitto are:

 Multiple config files:
 ConfigHelloWorld.yaml defines the smallest possible Kitto x application, the classic "Hello World".
 Config.yaml is the HelloKitto application itself.
 ConfigEmbedded.yaml shows how to embed (part of) a Kitto x application in an existing web page through an iframe.
 FireDAC-based database connection to SQL Server, PostgreSQL or Firebird (selectable via in ).
 JWT authentication ( with a envelope) — stateless authentication envelope: signed token in an HttpOnly cookie, no server-side session-id lookup. The authenticator stays in charge of the credential check (MD5-hashed passwords in ). No / no environment combo on the login page: the active backend is whatever resolves to. See ConfigAuthJWT.
 DB authentication using a standard database table and hashed passwords.
 With defaults.
 HTMX theming.
 Localization.
 Models and model relationships (references and details).
 Cascade delete — declares on its detail, so deleting a party deletes its invitations with it, in the same transaction. Without that node the delete is refused with a message naming the record and counting what refers to it. See Deleting a master that has details.
 Tree-based or Toolbar-based menu.
 Tree menu with three levels
 Tile menu for Smartphone and Tablet
 Custom logo through the use of an HtmlPanel controller.
 Tabbed views (TabPanel controller).
 StatusBar controller.
 Data display and editing with rules.
 List grouping with a custom javascript template.
 Party calendar — the same model shown on a month/week/day calendar through a whose is a CalendarPanel. See The Party calendar view below.
 List filtering with multiple user filters.
 A custom form layout.
 Master/Detail display and edit forms.
 Input writing in grid
 Record coloring in grid
 Rules to Prevent Adding and Prevent Deleting records 
 different kind of form views:
 new record in a tabpanel from menu
 new record from popup menu 

 The Party calendar view 

The Parties menu folder offers the parties both as a grid (Party list, view ) and as a calendar (Party calendar, view ). Both views read the same model and open the same edit form, so a party created in the grid shows up on the calendar and vice versa.

 A date and a time combined into one DateTime field. The table stores the date ( ) and the start time ( ) in two columns. The calendar needs a single start instant, so adds a hidden expression field that works on every supported database engine through the macro:

title: Help Chat (in-app assistant)
summary: The Help Chat is a conversational assistant for the end user of a Kitto x  application: a floating bubble in the bottom-right corner that opens a chat drawer where the user can ask how to do things ("how do I export a grid?", "what is this screen for?") and get an answer. (see the picture below).
text:
Help Chat (in-app assistant)

The Help Chat is a conversational assistant for the end user of a Kitto x 
application: a floating bubble in the bottom-right corner that opens a chat drawer where the user can
ask how to do things ("how do I export a grid?", "what is this screen for?") and get an answer. (see the picture below).

It is not a chat between users — it is a per-user help assistant. The way answers are produced is
 pluggable: out of the box a deterministic provider searches the KittoX documentation and links the
relevant page; an AI backend (Claude, grounded on the docs) is switchable from config with no code
change.

 tip Two steps, not one
A YAML flag turns the assistant on — , with the answer engine chosen by
 — but the units that implement it are opt-in from , like every
other optional subsystem. Enabling the flag without linking them stops the application at startup
with an error naming the exact unit to add.

 Enabling it

 1. Turn it on in :

With (default) nothing is shown. The bubble appears only on the authenticated page.

 2. Link the units from your — the endpoint unit plus the provider you configured:

Help Chat is not part of (the core umbrella): it is a feature subsystem with its
own background workers, linked only into the applications that use it — an application that does not
use the assistant carries neither its code nor the Markdown library behind it. Linking the units while
 is costs only binary size; note though that the endpoints
are registered by the unit itself and are not gated by the flag.

If but the units are missing, the application fails fast at startup
( ) with an error naming the exact unit to add — the framework never
silently falls back to the stub for a forgotten unit:

 HelpChat is enabled in Config.yaml but its units are not linked into this application. Add
 "Kitto.Web.Handler.Chat" and a provider unit … to your project's UseKitto.pas.

 The HelpChat provider "claude" is configured in Config.yaml but is not registered. Add the unit
 Kitto.Chat.Provider.Claude to your project's UseKitto.pas.

The Notification Center behaves the same way: add .

 3. If your application compiles the framework sources (rather than using the 
package), add the Markdown library to the unit search path of the — 
renders the provider's answer through it:

 warning Add it to every , not just the one you build day to day
Desktop, service, ISAPI and Apache projects all compile the same , so they all need
the entry. A deployment project left behind gives no sign of it until someone actually rebuilds it,
and then fails with pointing at a unit that has nothing to do
with whatever was being changed. The sample applications carry the entry in all of their projects.

 What the user sees

 A floating assistant bubble (bottom-right). Clicking it opens a drawer with the conversation
 history and a composer (Enter to send, Shift+Enter for a new line, Esc to close). It uses the theme's
 Material icon and colours, matching the rest of the UI in light and dark.
 The user types a question; their message appears immediately, a typing indicator shows while the
 answer is produced on the server, then the assistant reply is displayed (links, bold and inline code
 are rendered). The conversation can be cleared from the drawer header.
 Contextual help: on List and Form screens a ? button in the toolbar opens the chat with a
 question about that screen, anchored to the screen's controller type so the answer points to the
 matching documentation page. (When the chat is disabled, the ? button keeps its classic behaviour of
 opening a configured help URL in a new tab.)

 Answer providers

The provider is selected by name ( ); an unknown/empty name falls back to , so
the chat always has a working backend.

 Provider | Name | Behaviour |
 
 Stub | | Returns an honest placeholder. Validates the UI/flow with no dependency or key. |
 Doc search | | Searches the bundled KittoX documentation index and answers with the best page's summary

text:
Kitto x allows to create Rich Internet Applications based on a data model that can be mapped onto any database. The client-side part uses HTMX (through WebBroker technology) to create a fully AJAX application, allowing you to build standard and advanced data-manipulating forms in a fraction of the time.

 Kitto x is aimed at Delphi developers that need to create web or mobile applications without delving into the intricacies of HTML, CSS or Javascript, yet it allows access to the bare metal if required.

 Kitto x includes a database-agnostic data-access layer, allowing to create applications that work on any database engine and port applications between database engines.

A Kitto x application is described as a set of easily maintained YAML files, keeping definitions abstract and declarative and allowing for future extensions. Business rules are enforced either declaratively or through small javascript fragments on the client, or in Delphi code on the server.

 Kitto x was originally designed by Nando Dessena and its development is sponsored by Ethea and maintained by Carlo Barazzetta, which uses Kitto x for internal development projects and client work and provides Kitto x -related tools, support and development services.
