keywords: After the update: translate and compile
text:
Update Locale 

Keeping the GNU gettext files of an application in sync with the strings you mark for translation — scattered across YAML metadata and Delphi code — is tedious by hand. KIDE x automates it: with one command it scans the project's metadata and sources, extracts every translatable string, and merges the result into a language's — preserving the translations already done.

This is the recommended way to build and maintain the files of a Kitto x application: you mark strings with (and use the standard label nodes), then re-run this command whenever metadata or code changes. Translators working in parallel never lose their work.

 Why this matters 

A typical Kitto x application has hundreds of strings scattered across:

 YAML metadata — , , , labels, button/ToolView captions, dialog titles, filter labels
 Delphi source — strings inside calls in , , and your own units

Manually keeping the files aligned with all of this is impractical. KIDE x does it in seconds with two extraction passes merged into a single :

 What it extracts 

 1. YAML metadata 

KIDE x walks the loaded metadata catalog — Models, Views, Layouts and the top-level Config files — and collects a node's value when either:

 the node name is one of the configured localizable keys — by default , , , , , , (list read from in KIDE x 's ); or
 the node value is already wrapped as .

The wrapper is stripped, so the msgid is the plain text (e.g. → msgid ).

 tip Wrap everything you want translated
The name list above is intentionally small. Any other translatable YAML value must be wrapped in to be picked up — view , labels, filter captions, descriptions (never the DB codes), etc. For model fields the recommended form is an explicit , which is both extracted and self-documenting.

 tip Scaffolded views come out translatable
A View generated by KIDE x — the Create DataView… action, the DataView wizard, or the / MCP tools — no longer carries the filter captions in the language of whoever generated it. The composed (Search Dolls) is not written at all, so the grid falls back to the framework's own caption, which follows the session language; the free-text filter is written as , a plain msgid already in the framework catalog. Everything else you add by hand still needs the wrapper.

 danger Never wrap a value that is not shown to the user
The wrapper makes a value change with the session language. That is right for a label and wrong for anything the application matches, stores or emits. Leave these alone:

 Node | What it really is |
 
 | the XML element name wrapping a record set in ( ), used by the XML export and FOP report tools — not a label, despite the name |
 keys, filter keys | the codes stored in the database — translate the value after the colon, never the key |
 SQL comparison literals inside | and the like; only the displayed text in the same expression may be wrapped |
 , , , , , , , , , , rule parameters | table/column, file and object names |

The plural caption is a different node, , and that one you do wrap. See what must not be wrapped for the reasoning.

 2. Delphi sources 

KIDE x then runs the bundled dxgettext ( ) over the project's sibling folder, extracting every / string from your Delphi units into a temporary catalog.

 3. Merge 

The two passes are merged into the target language's with : existing values are kept, and strings found for the first time are added with an empty translation, ready to be filled in.

The operation is non-destructive — it only adds missing msgids; it never overwrites an existing translation.

 Scope 

 It maintains the application catalog only — per language. The framework strings ( ) are shipped translated by Ethea and are not regenerated here.
 It works on one language at a time: you run it on a specific .

 Prerequisites 

 A project open in KIDE x .
 The bundled dxgettext tools ( and ), shipped under . The folder is read from in KIDE x 's (default ) and shown read-only in the dialog.
 Project layout: (the

title: KIDEx Metadata Validation
summary: Because a Kitto x application is defined almost entirely in YAML metadata, a mistake in a  file — a mistyped node, a value of the wrong type, a reference to a view that does not exist — usually surfaces only at run time, when the page is opened. Metadata Validation moves those errors to design time: it reads every mode
keywords: How KIDEx helps you write correct YAML: the tree context menu
1. The annotation always declares the real runtime default
2. The tree menu proposes the meaningful value
3. The validator hints when a node equals its default
text:
KIDE x Metadata Validation

Because a Kitto x application is defined almost entirely in YAML metadata, a mistake in a
 file — a mistyped node, a value of the wrong type, a reference to a view that does not
exist — usually surfaces only at run time, when the page is opened. Metadata Validation moves
those errors to design time: it reads every model, view, layout and the , checks them
against what the framework actually understands, and reports problems before you run the app.

It is one of the most useful features for the day-to-day author of a Kitto x application,
and it is worth understanding well.

 tip One schema, two jobs
Validation is not a separate rulebook. It reads the same RTTI annotations that drive the tree
context menu (see KIDE x YAML Attributes). Annotating a class
therefore does two things at once: it fills the Add… menu, and it teaches the validator what a
correct file looks like.

 Running the validator

There are two ways to run exactly the same validation engine.

 Inside KIDE x 

Open a project and choose Validate Metadata (it also runs the Layout validator). The messages
panel is cleared, then filled with one line per finding, each tagged with a severity icon.

 A recap when it finishes. As soon as the run ends, KIDE x tallies the findings and
shows a summary — both as a final line in the panel and as a dialog you acknowledge:

 Validation complete: 1 error(s), 2 warning(s), 3 hint(s).

The dialog's icon reflects the worst severity found — an error stop, a warning triangle, or a plain
information mark when the metadata is clean — so you know the outcome at a glance without reading
every line.

 Double-click a finding to open the offending file. This is the fastest way to act on a result:
double-click any line and KIDE x opens — or brings to the front, if already open — the
editor for the model, view, layout or the message concerns, and moves the tree focus
straight onto the node being validated. A missing required node focuses its parent; a message that
is about the file as a whole focuses the root. Either way the "incriminated" file is one double-click
away, already scrolled to the right place.

 tip Re-run after refreshing
A finding remembers the exact object it came from. If you refresh the metadata (or reload the
project) after validating, those objects are rebuilt, so an old finding can no longer point at them:
double-clicking it then does nothing but show a short status note asking you to re-run the
validation. The list is always cleared and rebuilt at the start of each run, so a fresh validation
never carries stale links.

 Headless, from the command line (MCP-KittoX)

The console server MCP-KittoX exposes the same validator, which makes it easy to run in a build
pipeline or a pre-commit check:

It opens the project (a folder is resolved to its , in the root or in the 
sub-folder), prints one line per finding — prefixed error, warning, hint,
 info — followed by a summary, and returns exit code 2 when any error is found (0
otherwise). A typical run:

 Filter the panel by severity. Below the messages panel, the Filter Messages box has three
check boxes — Errors, Warnings, Hints. Untick one to hide that severity: with a handful
of errors buried in dozens of hints, hiding the hints lets you concentrate on what must be fixed.
Info/progress lines are always shown. The filter only changes what is displayed — the end-of-run
recap still counts every finding — and your choice is remembered across sessions.

 Severity levels

The validator classifies every finding into one of four levels. The distinction matters: an
 error is something that will not work; a warning is something to look at; a hint is a
tidy-up suggestion.

 Level | Meaning | Typical examples |
 
 Error | The file is wrong and the app will misbehave or fail to open the view. | Missing required node ( , ); a data view with no ; an enum value not in the allowed set; an integer node holding a non-number; a reference to a model, view or field that d

title: View & Layout Editor
summary: The View Editor and Layout Editor work together to define the user interface of a Kitto x application. Views define what data is shown and how it behaves; layouts define where fields are positioned in forms.
text:
View & Layout Editor 

The View Editor and Layout Editor work together to define the user interface of a Kitto x application. Views define what data is shown and how it behaves; layouts define where fields are positioned in forms.

 View Editor 

 Editor layout 

When you double-click a view in the project tree, KIDE x opens it in the editor panel:

The tree shows the complete view structure:
 Type — (for data-bound views) or (for menu views)
 Controller — the controller type ( , , , , etc.)
 MainTable — the primary data model and its field selection
 Fields — which model fields to include and their view-level overrides
 DetailTables — master/detail relationships for form tabs
 Controller settings — CRUD permissions, toolbar, filters, paging, ToolViews

 tip Read-only properties
A property that the metadata carries but the HTMX runtime does not honour yet is shown read-only rather than hidden: the value written in the YAML stays visible and can be copied, but it cannot be edited from the designer. It becomes editable again when the feature is wired up.

 Creating a view manually 

1. Right-click the Views node in the project tree
2. Select New View
3. Choose the view type (Data or Tree)
4. Enter a name for the YAML file
5. Use the tree editor and context menus to build the view structure

 DataView wizard 

For a data grid over one or more models, the DataView Wizard builds the views in one step and lets you edit them before they are saved:

1. Select one or more models in the project tree, right-click and select Create DataView…
2. The wizard builds an view for each of them and lists them on the left; the tree editor on the right edits the one selected, before anything is written
3. Press F2 on a view to rename it — the name becomes the file name, and a name already taken is shown in red
4. Click Finish — KIDE x writes one YAML file per view in the Views directory

Each view comes out as the builder makes it: , , a referencing the model with every field as a column, one detail table per detail reference, and a filter over the text fields.

 View wizard 

The DataView wizard covers one of the seven view builders. The View Wizard covers them all: the grid and the form, the grouped grid, the template panel, the chart, the calendar and the map. It opens from three places:

 right-click a model in the project tree and select Create View with the wizard…, with that model already chosen
 right-click the Views folder and select New View from a Model…
 the Metadata > View Wizard… menu

It has three pages:

1. Model and type. Pick the model — the box above the list filters it — and the type of view. Each type says what it produces and what it needs beyond the model.
2. Options. What that builder understands, and nothing else: the grouping field for a grouped grid, the label and value fields for a chart, the date fields for a calendar, the address fields for a map, the template for a template panel. The grid and the form have no options of their own. The view name is optional: left empty, the builder names the view itself.
3. Preview. The YAML that will be written, exactly as it will be written, with the resolved name and the target path. A name already taken is reported here and Finish stays disabled until you go back and change it.

 tip The wizard, the MCP tools and agree
Each page calls the same headless generator the tools of MCP-KittoX call, which in turn calls the framework's own view builder. So the wizard, an agent and a runtime expression all produce the same view — the shape is decided in one place, and the preview page shows it before anything is written.

What the wizard deliberately does not ask for: the subnodes no builder carries ( and the texts of a grouped grid — write them on the view afterwards), the Google Maps API key (it belongs to the application, in ), and the template file of a template panel (it is a resource, and goes in ).

 Layout Editor 

Layouts control how fields are arranged in form dialogs. Without a l

title: KIDEx YAML Attributes (RTTI-based property discovery)
summary: KIDE x YAML Attributes (RTTI-based property discovery)
keywords: How KIDEx resolves the class for a node
Validation is driven by the same annotations
How to annotate a new class
text:
KIDE x YAML Attributes (RTTI-based property discovery)

The KIDE x visual editor discovers YAML metadata properties at runtime via Delphi RTTI attributes declared on the framework classes.

A node that carries no RTTI metadata is therefore not listed in the right-click menu. It is not out of reach: Add custom node, the last entry of that menu, adds a node you name yourself, and that is how you write a key the editor does not describe yet.

When you right-click a node in the KIDE x tree editor, the popup menu is built dynamically by reading the RTTI annotations on the Delphi class that represents that node.

 Attribute types

 Kitto x defines six custom attribute classes in :

 YamlNode — Scalar properties

The most common attribute. Marks a property as mapped to a YAML node with an optional default value.

In KIDE x , scalar properties appear as "Add {NodePath}" or "Add {NodePath}: {Default}" menu items when the node is not yet present.

 Boolean defaults — annotation vs. menu {boolean-defaults-the-inverse-convention}

The default in is the real runtime default — the value the framework assumes when
the node is absent — for every type, booleans included. It is the single source of truth for
 "what does the framework do here by default?", and it is what lets the validator hint a node
that merely repeats its default (see Validation is driven by the same annotations).

The KIDE x menu, however, would gain nothing by offering a boolean node set to its own
default — the node would be a no-op. So for booleans only, and only when building the menu,
KIDE x proposes the opposite of the declared default, so Add always writes the
meaningful, behaviour-changing value. For strings, integers and enums there is no inversion: the
declared default is written as an editable starter (add , then change it).

 Node | default (real runtime default) | KIDE x Add writes |
 
 | | (hide) |
 | | (hide Add button) |
 | | |

The inversion is a single line inside KIDE x ( ), applied at
menu-build time; the annotation on the class is never touched. The runtime is unaffected either —
attributes are pure metadata, and getters keep their own fallback. See
the dedicated Metadata Validation page.

 YamlRequiredNode — Required scalar properties

Inherits from . Used for properties that must be present (e.g. , ).

Required nodes appear first in the popup menu.

 YamlContainer — Collection of N children

Marks a property as a container of homogeneous children (e.g. Fields, Rules). In KIDE x , containers are always visible in the menu with "Add {NodePath} child".

 YamlSubNode — Single config block

Marks a property as a sub-object with a fixed set of properties. KIDE x navigates into the sub-node class via RTTI to discover its own properties.

SubNode menu items appear only if the node is not already present: "Add {NodePath}".

 YamlChildType — Container child types

Applied to container classes (not properties) to list the types of children that can be added. Multiple attributes can be applied to the same class.

In KIDE x , child type entries always appear in the menu as "Add {Name}: {DefaultValue}" or "Add {Name}".

 YamlEnumValue — Enum value mapping

Applied to enumerated types to map ordinal values to YAML strings. Used by KIDE x to populate combo box drop-downs.

 How KIDE x resolves the class for a node

When you select a node in the KIDE x tree editor, KIDE x determines which framework class to query for RTTI:

 Node type | Resolution |
 
 , , , , , , | Direct class match |
 , , , | Direct class match (container classes) |
 , , | Direct class match |
 | Maps to |
 with name ending in "Controller" | Resolved via the controller registry |
 Any other | Automatic: walks up to the parent, reads its annotations, and returns the matching sub-node class |

The automatic parent-based resolution means that adding a annotation to a parent class is sufficient to make KIDE x discover the sub-node's properties — no hardcoded mapping needed.

 KIDE x popup menu behavior

title: Kittox at a glance
summary: Kitto x is a Delphi framework for building data-driven web applications. It combines a server-side engine written in Delphi with a modern client based on HTMX and server-generated HTML, allowing Delphi developers to create rich web interfaces without writing JavaScript.
text:
Kitto x at a glance

 Kitto x is a Delphi framework for building data-driven web applications. It combines a server-side engine written in Delphi with a modern client based on HTMX and server-generated HTML, allowing Delphi developers to create rich web interfaces without writing JavaScript.

The following diagram shows the overall architecture. Besides the HTML/HTMX browser UI, the same
server engine also exposes a REST/JSON API ( ) consumed directly by external clients — see
the REST channel in the diagram and the REST Server page.

 Kitto x might be the right tool for you if:

 You need to create a web front-end for a database with many tables;
 You want a rich user interface with search, filtering, grouping, charts, and more;
 You prefer to write your server-side business rules in Delphi;
 You need to deliver it rapidly;
 You want to do it with Open Source tools.

If some or all of the above conditions are met, then a closer look at Kitto x is in order.

 A closer look 

 Kitto x is an engine for creating data-driven web applications. This means that Kitto x offers tools to ease the creation of applications that display and allow to manipulate data stored in a database. It is made in Delphi, and it is mainly aimed at Delphi developers not wanting to learn the intricacies of HTML, CSS and Javascript but wanting to get the job done quickly.

As such, Kitto x is not a general-purpose tool for creating web sites.

A Kitto x application is based on a set of text files in yaml format called the Metadata. Metadata contains the mapped database objects (Models), the user interface descriptions (Views and Layouts) and the general configuration parameters such as database connection. A Kitto x application may as well contain business rules and controllers (custom user interface elements) written in Delphi.

 Kitto x roughly follows the MVC paradigm for data presentation.

 Kitto x offers the following features for application development:

 Scalable 3-tier architecture.
 Extensible metadata catalog based on yaml files.
 Database-agnostic data access.
 Modeling of database objects through Models.
 Server-side store with record state tracking, transactional master-detail saving, and blob lazy-loading.
 Pluggable authentication mechanisms.
 Pluggable access control/user permission management mechanisms.
 Modeling of presentation (user interface) elements through Views and Layouts.
 Pre-defined and pluggable Controllers.
 Attribute-based (RTTI) URL routing, extensible per application.
 REST/JSON web service exposing the same Models/Views, business rules and ACL over HTTP verbs ( ).
 Pervasive, pluggable macros throughout metadata.
 Built-in localization for multi-language applications.

 Kitto x integrates with other tools to implement some of its features:

 HTMX for the client-side user interface.
 WebBroker as a web server.
 dxgettext for localization.

For more information, please read the Getting started guide, download the source code and the examples, and if you have doubts just ask!

title: Introduction
summary: This page lists coding standards to be used for writing Kitto x code. This is meant to keep a coherent code base, style-wise, throughout the framework.
text:
Introduction 

This page lists coding standards to be used for writing Kitto x code. This is meant to keep a coherent code base, style-wise, throughout the framework.

 Indentation and structure 

Indent is two spaces. No tabs.
Code lines may be long up to about 80-100 characters. Continuation lines are indented. Do not ever wrap after ":" or ")", and before ";" or "(".

The "begin" and "end" keywords are always on their own line. Same for "else" (exception: "else if").

Assert() calls should be abundant at the beginning of routines to perform basic checks on input arguments and other preconditions (after the "inherited" call) and separated by actual statements by a blank line.
Assert() calls at the end of a function to check for assigned/valid Result and other postconditions are welcome where applicable (again, after a blank line).
Use blank lines liberally to separate blocks of code but beware of monster methods.

Use xmldoc comments to document what a piece of code does. Use in-code comments to document unobvious things ONLY, such as why something had to be done in a certain way.

If you find yourself writing a comment describing what the following piece of code does, consider refactoring out the code block in a new method (or local routine) and let the method name be the comment you were about to write.

In uses clauses:
 Always wrap and indent after the "uses" keyword.
 Order units according to the following scheme whenever possible: first RTL units, then library units, then EF units, then Kitto x units, then Kitto.Html units, each group in its own line.

All function arguments should be declared "const" when possible (exceptions tolerated for arguments of anonymous methods of TProc<> and TFunc<> type).
Output arguments are "out" and input/output arguments are "var". No exceptions.

If you feel you need to change a function argument locally, declare a local variable instead.

Always wrap and indent after "begin" and "var".

Always use try/finally blocks whenever a symmetric operation must take place (such as Create/Free, Disable /Enable , etc.).

Don't reference units from upper layers. A Kitto.Metadata. unit must not reference any Kitto.Html. unit. A EF. unit must not reference any Kitto x . units, and so on.

In class declarations, prefer "strict private" and "strict protected" specifiers. Don't use the legacy protected hacks (unit-level visibility) unless absolutely needed.
Define a "public" section with all the public members meant to be used by the class user and put it at the end of the class declaration.
Plus, (this might seem weird) define an additional "public" section and put it before the other one if you need to add scaffolding or methods not meant for public consumption, such as overrides of AfterConstruction or Destroy.

 Naming and capitalization 

All framework units are named Kitto x . or Kitto.X. where X is an area name (such as Metadata, Html, Auth, Tool, etc.). Units outside an area are considered of general use (such as Kitto.Types).
Units named EF. are lower level and not Kitto-specific.

Type naming rules reflect Delphi's classic naming. T prefix for classes, E for exceptions, I for interfaces, and CamelCaps everywhere. All Kitto x classes use a TK prefix. All EF classes use a TEF prefix.
 Kitto x HTML controller classes use a TKX prefix (e.g., , ).

Data values (variables, class fields, function arguments) all have a prefix:
 L for locals.
 A for function arguments.
 F for class fields.
The only exception is the I local variable which may be used as loop counter (a standard LSomething is also acceptable for this purpose).
Extremely rare implementation-level global variables might be prefixed with " ".

No interface-level global variables, ever.

All keywords are all lowercase; "string" is a keyword; "Integer" and "Boolean" are not.

 YAML Attributes 

All metadata and controller classes should be annotated with YAML attributes for KIDE RTTI discovery. See KIDE YAML Attributes for the full reference

text:
Introduction 

This document describes Kitto x 's standard conventions for setting up Delphi, and how to change them for custom setups.

 Kickstart a new application 

The recommended way to start a new application is the New Project Wizard, which scaffolds the complete project tree for you — the folder with an initial , the files for the deployment modes you pick (Standalone, Desktop, ISAPI, Apache), the supporting units ( , , ) with the database drivers you select, and the JWT authentication wiring. It is reachable from three entry points:

 KIDE x standalone — menu File > New Project;
 RAD Studio IDE plugin (with installed) — File > New > Other > KittoX Projects;
 MCP-KittoX — an AI agent calling the tool.

All three produce byte-identical output. See New Project Wizard for the full walk-through of every wizard page and the resulting directory layout.

After the wizard finishes you typically import your tables with the Model Wizard, generate List/Form views, and click Start to preview the app in your browser.

 tip Manual alternative
If you prefer not to use the wizard, you can still bootstrap by hand: copy the directory structure of HelloKitto (or another example application), open the project file and save it under a new name, then edit and start creating your own metadata files.

When running the compiled application, beware that it will try to run as a service if under an administrator account. To force the application to run with a visible GUI, pass as a command line argument.

If instead you want a detailed description of what's where and what you can customize — the standard directory layout, the Application Home and System Home paths, how the project finds Kitto x — read on.

 Details 

A Kitto x application is made up of a Delphi project that you create and maintain, a Home folder with metadata and resources (such as images or javascript files), and a link to the Kitto x sources or precompiled files.

 Standard directory layout 

As you can see in the HelloKitto example, a typical folder structure goes like this (KittoX targets Win64 only, with a single per deployment — no per-Delphi-version subfolders):

 HelloKitto
 Home
 Metadata
 Models
 Views
 Config.yaml
 Resources
 application.css
 HelloKitto.exe (the compiled application)
 Source
 UseKitto.pas
 Controllers.pas
 Rules.pas
 Projects
 HelloKitto.dpr/.dproj (Standalone)
 HelloKittoDesktop.dpr/.dproj (Desktop, WebView2)
 HelloKittoISAPI.dpr/.dproj (ISAPI)
 modhellokitto.dpr/.dproj (Apache module)
 Lib

Your application code goes into and , and the project file should be configured to output the compiled dcu files into a subdirectory of :

 Unit output directory = ..\Lib\$(Platform) 

and the exe file into :

 Output directory = ..\Home 

(both paths are relative to the folder). This is the layout the New Project Wizard generates for you.

This folder contains your yaml metadata and support files as well, and is called the Application Home.

 The Application Home path 

The Application Home is assumed to the your executable's directory. You can change this (for example when using a single Kitto x executable to serve different applications) in the following ways:

 By passing a argument on the command line.
 By setting the property at application startup.

 Finding Kitto x : The System Home path 

 contains the predefined metadata and support files, such as Kitto x 's default style sheet, CSS, JavaScript libraries, SVG icons, and HTML templates, which are used by your Kitto x application at run time and you shouldn't need to touch. This is called the System Home.

As you can see, the application needs to have Kitto x inside its directory structure. This is done to allow different applications to use different versions of the library without stepping on each other's toes, and to make the application as much self-contained as possible.

The project should be configured to find Kitto x , either in source format:

 Search path = ..\..\Externals\KittoX\Source; 
..\..\E

text:
REST Server

A Kitto x application can expose its data views as a REST/JSON web service, in parallel
to the HTML x GUI, under the versioned base path . It runs on the same
 and attribute router as the GUI, so the same YAML metadata, the same business rules
( ) and the same ACL apply — a record created over REST behaves exactly like one entered in a
form.

Like the Web Server, the REST server has no dedicated process: it is served
by whatever deployment mode the app runs in (standalone, service, console, ISAPI, Apache).

The base path is the default and can be changed in with
 (e.g. ); it applies to the whole REST tree (endpoints, token, OpenAPI,
Swagger UI) at runtime, no recompile needed.

 Request flow

 The router and are the same ones the GUI uses — the REST tree is just another
 set of attribute-decorated handlers ( / / / / ), not a parallel server.
 (in the core, no JSON dependency) is the shared CRUD service: it resolves the
 view, enforces the ACL and the model-level write flags, applies field/record rules and persists.
 The GUI form endpoints and the REST endpoints both flow through the same domain logic.
 is the serialization seam; the default uses the RTL
 (correct escaping, zero third-party dependencies).
 turns any exception on an path into a JSON envelope
 with a real HTTP status ( / / / / / / ).

 Enabling it (opt-in)

The REST support is opt-in and adds no JSON framework to a browser-only app. Add the umbrella unit
to your , exactly as you opt into :

An app that does not reference exposes no routes and links no REST code.

 The three layers

 Unit | Package | Role |
 
 ( ) | Core (no JSON) | Shared CRUD service: view resolution, ACL, / , rule sequence, . Used by both the GUI and REST. |
 ( , , , , ) | Opt-in | The handlers, the JSON serializer and the JSON error filter. |
 ( , ) | Opt-in | OpenAPI 3.0 spec generated from the metadata with System.JSON (no Neon). |
 (planned) | Opt-in² | Only if the API ever exposes typed Delphi DTO endpoints: mapping via delphi-neon. Not needed for the metadata-driven API or for OpenAPI. |

 Endpoints, permissions and authentication

The endpoint table, query parameters ( ), the model-level permission
flags ( , / / ) and the Bearer-token flow
( → ) are documented in full on the
REST API (JSON) reference page.

The API also describes itself: returns an OpenAPI 3.0 document
generated from the metadata, and serves an interactive Swagger UI page
(vendored, works offline). See REST API — OpenAPI / Swagger UI.

The online demos expose their REST API too — try the live Swagger UI without installing anything:
HelloKitto ·
TasKitto (see the live demos page for
credentials).

 Deploying under IIS / Apache

The framework serves the REST API identically on every transport, but IIS and Apache may block the
write verbs ( / / ) before the request reaches the app:

 IIS — remove the WebDAV module for the app and allow the verbs on the ISAPI handler mapping.
 Apache — allow the verbs in the /module configuration.

The Indy hosts (Standalone / Service / Console)
accept all verbs out of the box — KittoX installs an Indy passthrough so the
 scheme is not rejected as "Unsupported authorization scheme". No configuration needed.

 Cross-origin browser clients (CORS)

A browser page on a different origin needs CORS. It is off by default; enable it per-app under
 in ('' or a comma-separated list, optional
 ). KittoX then answers the preflight and adds the 
headers on responses. See REST API — CORS.

 Extending it

 is . To customize a single endpoint (or add a hook) for one application,
subclass it and register the subclass with in your
 section — the same mechanism used for the GUI view handler. See
Attribute-Based Routing — overriding an endpoint.

 See also

 REST API (JSON) — the full endpoint / auth / error reference
 Web Server Configuration — the shared engine and deployment modes
 Attribute-Based Routing — how the router and work

text:
Web Server Configuration

A Kitto x application can be deployed in several forms, as it supports Delphi's WebBroker architecture. All deployment modes share the same core engine ( ), so your YAML metadata, controllers and business logic work identically everywhere.

You don't need a separate web server for development (although you can use one in production, as explained in the Proxy page).

 Deployment Modes

 Mode | Entry point | HTTP server | Threading | Best for |
 
 Desktop GUI | | Indy ( ) | Thread pool (default 20) | Development, debugging, single-user |
 Windows Service | | Indy ( ) | Thread pool (default 20) | Production standalone |
 Console | | Indy ( ) | Thread pool (default 20) | Docker, headless servers |
 IIS (ISAPI DLL) | | IIS via WebBroker | IIS thread pool | Enterprise Windows hosting |
 Apache module | | Apache via WebBroker | Apache thread pool | Linux/cross-platform hosting |

 auto-detects whether the process is running as a Windows Service or as a desktop GUI application.

For detailed deployment instructions for each mode, see the dedicated pages:

 Standalone (Desktop GUI)
 Windows Service
 Console (Headless)
 ISAPI (IIS) — step-by-step IIS setup with Application Pool, handler mapping, permissions
 Apache Module
 Desktop Embedded (WebView2)

 The WebBroker Bridge

For ISAPI and Apache deployments, the bridge between WebBroker and the Kitto x engine consists of two units:

 — A with a single default handler:

 — Singleton that owns the :

To use ISAPI or Apache, include in your uses clause and set . No additional code is needed.

 Client-side Libraries

 Kitto x includes all required client-side libraries (HTMX, CSS, Material Design Icons) inside its path, so you don't need to provide them separately. Icons are stored in with 5 style variants (filled, outlined, round, sharp, two-tone).

title: Deployment
summary: This page provides an overview of all deployment modes available for Kitto x applications. For development setup, see Web Server Configuration.
text:
Deployment

This page provides an overview of all deployment modes available for Kitto x applications. For development setup, see Web Server Configuration.

 Application directory

When deploying a Kitto x application, you need to provide its Application Home directory with the executable file and the and subdirectories.

During development, the Application Home and System Home directories are separated. In deployment, it is recommended that you merge them together, keeping the Application Home files in case of duplicates. Use an installer tool like InnoSetup to automate this.

The client-side libraries served under (HTMX, Alpine.js, the icons, , , …) live in the System Home , so the merge must include them — otherwise the pages load without their assets. In particular, if your application exposes the REST API with Swagger UI ( ), make sure these two files are present in the deployed :

If you deploy only the Application Home (without merging the System Home), copy the required framework assets into the app's own — the static route serves first, then falls back to the System Home (which may be absent in production).

 Choosing a deployment mode

 Mode | Executable | HTTP Server | Best for | Guide |
 
 Standalone (GUI) | | Indy (embedded) | Development, small deployments | Standalone |
 Windows Service | (same binary) | Indy (embedded) | Production on Windows | Windows Service |
 Service + Proxy | + nginx/Apache/IIS | Indy + reverse proxy | Production with HTTPS, multiple apps | Windows Service, Proxy |
 Console | (separate ) | Indy (embedded) | Docker, headless servers | Console |
 IIS (ISAPI DLL) | | IIS via WebBroker | Enterprise Windows hosting | ISAPI (IIS) |
 Apache module | / | Apache via WebBroker | Linux / cross-platform | Apache |
 Desktop Embedded | | Indy + WebView2 | Desktop app look & feel | Desktop Embedded |

All modes use the same YAML metadata, the same controllers, and the same core. The choice only affects how the HTTP server is hosted and managed.

 tip Develop on Desktop, deploy by switching the host
While you build your application, always run it in Standalone (Desktop GUI) mode. It is an
ordinary Delphi , so you launch it straight from the IDE under the debugger: breakpoints
in your rules and controllers, step-through, and the live request log in the main window.

Because every mode shares the same YAML, the same controllers and the same , moving to
the final deployment mode does not touch your application code — you switch only the host unit
(the entry point): for Desktop / Service, for Console,
 for ISAPI / Apache. The Windows Service even uses the same binary as the
Desktop GUI. In short: develop on Desktop, deploy by changing one unit.

 Service + Proxy vs native modules

For production deployments, you can choose between:

 Service + Proxy: the application runs as a Windows Service with its own Indy HTTP server; a reverse proxy (nginx, Apache, or IIS ARR) forwards requests. Each app can be restarted independently without affecting the web server or other apps.
 Native modules (ISAPI/Apache): the application runs as a DLL loaded directly by the web server. Simpler setup (no proxy) but requires a full web server restart to update the DLL or reload YAML metadata.

See Windows Service Deployment for the proxy approach and Proxy Configuration for nginx/Apache/IIS setup details.

 Common configuration

Regardless of deployment mode, every Kitto x application uses for:

 Database connection (see Database Configuration)
 Authentication and access control (see Authentication)
 Session timeout and cleanup
 Theme, charset, localization

Session configuration applies to all modes:

 Application tools

If your application uses one of the following tools, install the required software on the server:

 Tool | Requirement |
 
 ADOTool (Excel export) | ADO/OLEDB provider |
 FlexCel (Excel export) | FlexCel commercial license (TMS) |
 ReportBuilder | ReportBuilder commercial license (Digital Metaphors) |
 PDFMerge |

text:
Kitto x Enterprise 

 Kitto x Enterprise is the commercial edition of Kitto x , designed for teams that build complex business applications on tight delivery schedules and need a complete set of advanced controllers, visual development tools and integrations beyond what the Open-Source core provides.

The Open-Source edition under Apache 2.0 is and stays a complete framework for building data-driven web applications. The Enterprise edition adds the productivity layer: less time wiring infrastructure, more time delivering features.

 Why choose Enterprise? 

If your project hits any of these scenarios, the Enterprise edition is what you are looking for:

 You want to prototype the data layer in hours, not days — KIDE reverse-engineers your database into Kittoˣ models, scaffolds menus, generates layouts, validates YAML metadata in real time.
 Your application needs rich data visualisation — interactive charts, calendars, maps and auto-refreshing dashboards already integrated as of any , with no third-party JavaScript plumbing to maintain.
 Your customers ask for PDF and Excel reports — server-side rendering through ReportBuilder Enterprise (with DataPipeline / RAP) and TMS FlexCel (template-based, formulas, advanced formatting).
 You ship desktop-style applications on Windows — wrap your Kittoˣ app inside a native window via WebView2, no browser, no address bar, full desktop UX.
 You need fine-grained, function-level access control — the Enterprise profiling layer extends the base Access Control with per-function permissions for back-office scenarios.
 You want commercial licensing, indemnification and priority support — closed-source distribution rights and direct support from the team that builds Kittoˣ.

 What is included 

 Visual development — KIDE 

 KIDE, the Kittoˣ Visual IDE, replaces hand-written YAML with a tree-based editor whose property menus are generated at runtime from Delphi RTTI — always in sync with the framework.

 Project management — wizards to create new projects, project tree, run/preview integration
 Model editor — reverse-engineer database tables, generate and update models
 View & Layout editor — visual grid and form designers with auto-generation
 Config editor — edit with discovery of every setting
 YAML attributes reference — how RTTI metadata drives the IDE

 Advanced Web GUI controllers 

A library of controllers ready to plug into any view as , with consistent styling, theme support and grid sidebar integration:

 Controller | Purpose |
 
 ChartPanel | Interactive Bar / Line / Pie / Doughnut charts via Chart.js, with grid sidebar and live filter integration |
 CalendarPanel | Month / week / day calendar with color-coded events, drag-and-drop rescheduling |
 GoogleMap | Markers from address fields via Google geocoding, routing, bidirectional grid-map interaction |
 Dashboard | Responsive grid of KPI cards, charts and views with JavaScript-driven auto-refresh |

 Enterprise reporting and export 

 ReportBuilderTool — server-side PDF generation through ReportBuilder Enterprise using DADE / RAP and AutoSearch parameters, sharing the Kittoˣ database connections
 ExportExcelTool — Excel export via ADO (Open-Source) or via TMS FlexCel (Enterprise), with template files, formulas and advanced formatting
 MergePDFTool — PDF composition through Debenu QuickPDF (available in both editions)

 Desktop Embedded Mode 

 Desktop Embedded Mode wraps the Kittoˣ application inside a native VCL window using (WebView2). Same web codebase, fully native window chrome, single-instance management, automatic title binding from . Ideal for line-of-business apps where customers expect a desktop-class experience.

 Advanced user/function profiling 

The Enterprise edition extends the base Access Control with fine-grained function-level profiling — permissions can be attached to specific functions or business operations, not just resources. See Enterprise Components for details.

 InstantSolutions Framework integration 

 Ins

text:
Enterprise Components

 Kitto x Enterprise includes advanced components not available in the Open-Source edition. These components extend the framework with additional tools, report engines, and development features.

For a complete comparison between the two editions, see the Feature Matrix. For the commercial overview of the Enterprise edition (why choose it, pricing, contact) see Kittoˣ Enterprise.

 Desktop Embedded Mode

The Desktop Embedded Mode allows wrapping a Kitto x application inside a native Windows desktop window using Microsoft Edge WebView2 ( ). The application looks and behaves like a traditional desktop application — no address bar, no tabs, no bookmarks.

 Report and Export Tools

 ReportBuilder Tool

The ReportBuilder Tool controller generates reports using the ReportBuilder Enterprise engine. It supports server-side report rendering with optional design mode for end-user customization.

 warning
Requires a separate commercial license from Digital Metaphors.

 FlexCel Export Tool

The ExportExcelTool controller with FlexCel support generates Excel files using the TMS FlexCel engine. It supports advanced formatting, formulas, and template-based export.

 warning
Requires a separate commercial license from TMS Software.

 DebenuQuickPDF Tool

The MergePDFTool controller uses the Debenu QuickPDF library for PDF merging and manipulation, including QR code generation and document composition. The Debenu library is Win32 only (so this tool runs in 32-bit builds only) and is planned to be replaced by an equivalent library supporting both 32-bit and 64-bit — see the MergePDFTool page.

 KIDE — The Kitto x IDE

KIDE is a dedicated development environment for Kitto x applications. It provides:

 Two-way YAML editor — edit metadata as tree or raw YAML, changes sync both ways
 Model import and generation — import database tables as Kitto x models with automatic field mapping
 View and Layout visual editor — drag-and-drop grid columns and form fields with auto-generation
 Menu and Home view creation — scaffold the application structure from models
 Code-checking — validate YAML metadata against the current model definitions
 Resource editor — manage images, JavaScript, and CSS files

For details, see the KIDE documentation.

 Advanced User/Function Profiling {advanced-user-function-profiling}

The Enterprise edition includes enhanced user profiling capabilities with fine-grained function-level access control, extending the base Access Control system.

 InstantSolutions Framework Integration {instantsolutions-framework-integration}

 Kitto x Enterprise integrates with the InstantSolutions Framework for building complex business applications with advanced data management patterns.

title: KIDEx: the KittoX IDE
summary: tip Kitto x Enterprise feature KIDE is part of the Kittoˣ Enterprise edition. See the Feature Matrix for the full comparison with the Open-Source edition.
text:
KIDE x : the KittoX IDE 

 tip Kitto x Enterprise feature
KIDE is part of the Kittoˣ Enterprise edition. See the Feature Matrix for the full comparison with the Open-Source edition.

 KIDE x is the visual development environment for Kitto x applications. It provides a tree-based YAML editor with context-sensitive property menus, database reverse engineering, project creation wizards, and an integrated HTTP server for live preview.

 Key features 

 Tree-based metadata editor — Models, Views, Layouts and Config files are displayed as navigable trees. Each node can be expanded, edited, and enriched via right-click context menus.
 RTTI-based property discovery — Context menus are built dynamically from the framework's metadata classes, ensuring they are always in sync with the controllers and properties available in your installed version of Kitto x .
 Database reverse engineering — Import table structures from any supported database (FireDAC, ADO, DBExpress) and generate Model YAML files automatically.
 Database generation from Models — The reverse direction: the Database Wizard generates and runs the DDL that brings the database in line with the project's Models, with an editable preview and multi-dialect support. See its limitations.
 Project wizards — Create new Kitto x projects from templates (Empty, Basic) with a guided wizard that generates the , , and folder structure.
 YAML syntax highlighting — Integrated SynEdit-based editor with YAML syntax highlighting, code folding, and auto-indentation.
 Validation driven by RTTI — Models, Views and Layouts are validated against the annotations on the framework classes themselves: node names, nested attributes and enum values, with unknown nodes reported as warnings. See YAML Attributes.
 Integrated HTTP server — Start/stop the Kitto x server directly from KIDE and preview the application in your browser without leaving the IDE.
 Layout preview — Visual preview of form layouts before running the application.
 Scalable, DPI-aware icons and themes — The whole icon set is multi-resolution and follows the monitor DPI; a theme selector previews the twelve VCL styles live, and the editor colours follow the chosen light or dark theme.
 Check for updates — KIDE x can check for a newer KittoX release and download and install the setup.

 Requirements 

 Delphi 10.4 or later (RAD Studio)
 Kitto x Enterprise Edition license
 A supported database server for reverse engineering

 Quick start 

1. Launch KIDE x ( )
2. Open an existing project folder (the directory of a Kitto x application) or create a new one via File > New Project
3. The tree panel on the left shows the project structure: Models, Views, Layouts, Config
4. Double-click any item to open it in the editor
5. Right-click a tree node to see available properties and child nodes
6. Click Start to launch the integrated server and preview the application

 RAD Studio IDE plugin 

KIDE x ships a design-time package — — that integrates the New Project Wizard directly into the RAD Studio IDE. Once the package is installed (Component → Install Packages → Add → ), the wizard is reachable without launching KIDE x standalone:

 File > New > Other > KittoX Projects shows four entries — one per supported deployment mode:

 Gallery entry | Output |
 
 KittoX Windows App / Service (.exe) | Standalone executable (Indy embedded server) |
 KittoX Windows Desktop App (.exe) | Desktop executable with embedded WebView2 |
 KittoX ISAPI Module (.dll) | ISAPI library for IIS |
 KittoX Apache Module (.dll) | Apache 2.4 module |

Picking any entry opens the same five-page wizard form used by KIDE x standalone, with the deployment mode that matches the gallery entry already ticked and locked on the first page. At Finish the IDE opens the generated (the one that matches the picked mode) as a new project group, ready to compile.

The package also installs a YAML syntax highlighter for files inside the IDE editor, so editing , Models and Views from the Project Ma

Wizard would have written if you'd driven it visually.

 License gate | OnGuard, shared with KIDE x ; every tool method calls first; unlicensed → ( ) → JSON-RPC error visible to client |

Kitto x FAQ

This page collects frequently asked questions about the Kitto x framework. If you need an article covering a particular subject, or if you think you have something to contribute, let us know by posting in the issues section of this repository.

 General

 What is Kitto x ?

 Kitto x is a Delphi framework for building data-driven web applications. You define your data models, views, and layouts in declarative YAML files, and Kitto x generates a complete web application with server-rendered HTML, HTMX for dynamic updates, and AlpineJS for client-side interactivity.

 What Delphi versions are supported?

 Kitto x supports RAD Studio / Delphi 10.4 Sydney and later (11 Alexandria, 12 Athens, 13). The framework package projects are built per version, under , , , and . Your own application targets Win64 with a single per deployment mode (see New Project Wizard).

 Which databases does Kitto x support?

 Kitto x is database-agnostic through pluggable adapters: FireDAC (recommended, supports all major databases), DBExpress, and ADO/OLEDB. Configure the adapter in under .

 Can I use multiple databases in the same application?

Yes. Define multiple entries under in and use on models or for dynamic routing. See Multiple Databases.

 Application structure

 What is the minimum set of files for a Kitto x application?

A minimal application needs:
 A Delphi project file ( ) calling 
 referencing and any project-specific units
 with at least and a entry
 At least one Model ( in )
 At least one View ( in )
 A Home View defining the main layout

 What is the Home directory?

 is the runtime root for each application. The macro resolves to it. It contains (YAML files), (static assets), and optionally .

 How do I run my application?

Compile and run the Delphi project. It starts a built-in HTTP server on the port defined in ( , default 8080). Open a browser at .

 Models and Views

 What is the difference between a Model and a View?

A Model describes the data structure (fields, types, relationships, validation rules) and maps to a database table. A View describes the UI: which model to display, which fields to show, how to arrange them, and which controller to use.

 How do I create a reference (foreign key) field?

In your model YAML, add a field with type pointing to the referenced model:

This creates a lookup combo in the UI. See Referenced Fields.

 How do I add a detail table (master-detail)?

Add a section to your view's :

The detail table appears as a tab in the form editor.

 How do I make a field read-only, hidden, or required?

Set the corresponding property on the model field or view field:

View-level settings override model-level settings.

 Business rules

 What is a business rule in Kitto x ?

A rule is a piece of business logic, written in Delphi, that Kitto x applies during data entry. Rules can validate data (and block the operation with an error message), compute or set field values, react to a field change, or enforce cross-field/cross-record integrity before writing to the database. They are the place where the application's business logic lives, declaratively attached to the data model. See Business Rules for the full reference.

 How do I attach a rule to a model or a field?

Add a subnode and list the rule by name. You can attach rules at four levels: model, model field, view table, and view-table field. Field-level rules can be stacked and fire in declaration order:

A model-level rule is always applied; a view-level rule is applied only when editing through that view, in addition to the model rules. A view-table-field rule overrides the model-field rule of the same type.

 How do I write my own rule in Delphi?

Create a class descending from (unit ), override the lifecycle method(s) you need, and register it:

The YAML name is the class name without its leading (or ): → . The unit must be reachable from so its runs, and the app must be recompiled for the rule to take effect.

Getting started with Kitto x 

 Kitto x is compatible from Delphi 10.4 up to the latest version. The fastest way to see
what it can do is to try the four sample applications — HelloKitto,

 Sport Club Manager — either live in your browser or compiled and
running on your own machine.

There are two ways to get started, and you can mix them freely:

 Learn from the demos — compile and run a sample application, then read its YAML and Delphi
 code to see how the pieces fit together. Start here if you want to understand the framework.
 Build your own — scaffold a new application with the
 KIDE x wizard and point it at your database. Start here
 if you already know what you want to build.

Most newcomers begin with the demos.

 See it working right now — the live demos

The examples are published online, so you can explore a real Kitto x UI in your browser
with no setup at all:

 Open the live demos 
 — see the live demos page for the full credential list).

 Run the demos on your own machine

When you want to see the demos build and run in your environment, all you need is:

 Delphi 10.4 or later — any edition, Professional included. The bundled FireDAC/dbExpress
 client-server drivers (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle, remote Firebird) require Delphi
 Enterprise/Architect; on Professional you reach a client/server DBMS through a third-party
 provider such as ODAC (already supported via ). See
 supported Delphi versions and editions.
 A development database server to host the example's data. Each example ships ready-made
 scripts to create and populate its database on SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Firebird or Oracle.

You do not need to install any Kitto x package into the IDE: the framework has no
design-time components, so there is nothing to register — you just open an example project, compile
and run it, then navigate to it in a browser.

 Compiling and running the demos — the full walkthrough: preparing the
 database, the unit that enables the database engines, and pointing an example at your
 own database.

After looking at the examples, dive into Kitto x 's basic concepts.

 Creating your own application 

When you are ready to build your own application, first set up your development environment:

 Configuring Delphi
 Configuring the Web Server

Then the recommended path is the visual tooling in KIDE x :

 1. New Project Wizard — scaffolds the complete project ( , , , ) for the deployment modes you pick.
 1. Model Wizard — reverse-engineers Models from your existing database tables.
 1. DataView Wizard — generates a data grid from each of those Models, and the
 View Wizard does the same for any of the
 other view types: form, grouped grid, template panel, chart, calendar, map.

You can then refine everything visually in the Config Editor, Model Editor and View & Layout Editor. Prefer to work by hand? See the manual alternative in Configuring Delphi.

 tip Start in Desktop mode, deploy later
When the wizard asks which deployment modes to generate, pick Standalone (Desktop GUI) for
development: it runs as an ordinary Delphi under the debugger, so you can breakpoint your
rules and controllers. You can add the production modes (Windows Service, ISAPI, Apache…) at any
time — they share the very same YAML and code and differ only in the host unit. See
Deployment.

Happy Kittoing!

 Core — Apache 2.0

All source files in Kitto x Core are licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. You may use, modify, and distribute them for any purpose — commercial or non-commercial — without restriction.

 Enterprise Modules — AGPL-3.0 / Commercial

Enterprise modules are dual-licensed:

1. AGPL-3.0 — free for applications released under a compatible open-source license with full source disclosure (including SaaS/web apps accessed over a network).

 No packages to install

global library path. Each shipped example already references the framework source folders on

text:
LanguageSwitcher 

 is the controller that renders the interface-language chooser: a small drop-down showing the current language's flag and native name, with a menu of every language the application ships. It is the companion of the ThemeSwitcher and is placed the same way — dropped into a layout region via YAML — so it can appear identically on the login page and inside the home.

 How it works 

Unlike the theme (a purely client-side preference), the language is a server-side, per-session setting driven by GNU gettext. Picking a language therefore does a short round-trip:

1. The menu item calls (in ).
2. That posts to the anonymous endpoint , which validates the code and stores it on the session.
3. The client reloads the current page, and the whole UI re-renders in the chosen language.

Because the endpoint is anonymous, the switcher works before sign-in too, so a visitor can pick their language and then log in.

 Available languages 

The list of offered languages is discovered, not configured, and discovery follows two rules:

 a language is offered when the application's holds at least one compiled catalog ( ), plus English (the source language, which needs no catalog);
 the framework's is not scanned. Its catalogs keep translating the framework's own strings, but they no longer make a language selectable on their own.

Adding a language is therefore a matter of putting the application's compiled catalog in place — see Adding a new language.

 warning Why both rules matter
A bare folder — or one holding only the source — would otherwise add French to the menu and translate nothing: the user picks it and the page comes back unchanged.

And since KittoX ships framework catalogs for , , and , an application translated only into Italian and Spanish would otherwise offer German and Portuguese as well — choosing one would produce a half-translated screen: framework chrome translated (Passwort, Sprache) with every application label still in the source language.

Each language id is mapped to a native display name and an ISO 3166 country code for the flag SVG under :

 Id | Name | Flag |
 
 | English | |
 | Italiano | |
 | Deutsch | |
 | Español | |
 | Português | |
 | Français | |

Any other id falls back to the up-cased code as the name and the code itself as the flag. Region variants such as are matched to their base language ( ) for the flag and name.

The current session language is preselected in the menu; a region-qualified session language (e.g. ) is matched to its base entry.

 Enabling it 

The switcher is gated by the same flag that governs per-session language:

 With the controller renders; with (or when fewer than two languages are available) it emits nothing and the container collapses — so you can drop it in defensively.
 With an empty , the initial language is auto-detected from the browser's ; the switcher then lets the user override it. See Choosing the language.

 Placing it 

Drop the controller into any layout region:

Typical placements (as in the shipped examples):

 Login — as a labelled field row inside the form (the framework renders it there automatically when , with the Language label on the left), or in a region of the login dialog.

 Home — at the bottom of the left menu, next to the ThemeSwitcher. In the examples both share a small chrome band:

 Styling 

The switcher's markup uses the / / classes in . It is theme-aware and adapts to the context:

 On a chrome band ( ) it uses the light chrome text and its pop-up opens upward.
 Inside the login form ( ) it matches the other inputs (same border, radius and drop-down arrow as the Environment combo).

 Configuration summary 

 Key | Default | Effect |
 
 | | Render the switcher (and allow a per-session language). → hidden |
 | (empty) | Empty = auto-detect from the browser; a code forces that language |

 See also 

 Localization — the / system, language selection, browser detection
 Update Locale (KIDE x ) — generate/refresh the translation catal

title: List Controller

Adding a presenter beside the grid
The form of the current record beside the grid
text:
List Controller 

Displays a list of records of a data view, with options for filtering, viewing, editing and deleting records, and composes the presenters that show them.

The List is the data-list host. It owns what concerns the list of data: the filter panel (rendered above its content), the action flags ( , , ...), the lookup context. It does not draw the data itself: that is the job of the presenters it hosts in its regions, each showing the same filtered records in one way:

 Presenter | Shows | Typical use |
 
 GridPanel | a paged, sortable grid | the default Center of every List |
 ChartPanel | a Chart.js chart | , often with a GridPanel beside it |
 CalendarPanel | events on a calendar | |
 TemplateDataPanel | records rendered through an HTML template | (read-only) |
 Form | the current record | beside the grid |

Every presenter of the same List reads the same view table and the same filters: changing a filter or pressing Refresh reloads all of them.

 Composing the panels 

A List arranges its presenters in the five regions of a border layout: plus , , , . Each region is declared with a node whose value is the controller type, or with a node naming another view.

 The grid is the default Center 

 alone is a grid: when no is declared the List creates a GridPanel in its Center. A node without a value (only options as children) still means the grid, so this view is a grid with a View button:

 Replacing the grid 

Give a value to show the data another way. The options of the presenter go inside its region node:

 Adding a presenter beside the grid 

Put a second presenter in a side region. Here the chart is the Center and a real grid sits to its left, sharing the data; sizes the region and adds a draggable splitter (TasKitto, ):

Any controller can go in a side region, not only a presenter: HelloKitto's view puts an legend in an .

 The form of the current record beside the grid 

A List can host the Form of the current record in one of its regions. The List keeps the form on the row selected in the grid, in view mode; Edit and Save happen in place, and after a save the grid reloads and the form shows the saved record again. This is TasKitto's view, complete:

Reading it top-down:

 belongs to the List: the search box filters both the grid and, through the selection, what the form shows.
 The Center is not declared, so it is the default GridPanel.
 hosts the form in the East region, 450 pixels wide, with a splitter. Its own shows a header above the form: a hosted presenter can have regions of its own.
 makes the grid load at once even though the view is also a lookup ( ). Opened as a lookup dialog the view shows only the grid: a modal List renders no regions.

How the hosted form behaves:

 When the view opens, the first row of the grid is selected and its record is shown in the panel. When the grid is empty the panel shows "No record selected.".
 Clicking a row loads that record into the panel. Sorting or paging the grid keeps the current record if its row is still there, otherwise the first row of the page is selected.
 With a hosted form, every form operation of the view (Add, Duplicate, Edit, View, double click) happens in the panel instead of a dialog. Delete re-aligns the panel to the first row.
 on the node selects a form layout other than the view table's, since a side panel usually wants fewer fields per row. (with ) puts the form under the grid instead.

This replaces Kitto1's option of the GridPanel, which is no longer read.

 Where the options go 

Options that govern the data belong at the level: , , , , , , , , . Options that govern one presentation go in that presenter's region node: , , , , , , . Options of the underlying table ( , , , , , ) stay under , where all presenters read them.

 Filters 

Filters allow the user to apply search predicates to lists of records. The node has a set of subnodes, each of which represents a filter of a specified type. Each filter renders a user interface (a search box

Localization

 Kitto x default language is English. Applications can be localized to any language using the GNU gettext system via dxgettext for Delphi.

Localization covers two layers:

1. Framework interface — buttons (Save, Cancel, Edit, Confirm, Close, etc.), error messages, dialog text
2. Application metadata — field labels, allowed values, view titles, hints defined in YAML

 File Structure

The framework locale folder is in . The application locale folder is in . At runtime, KittoX searches the application folder first, then the framework folder (same fallback pattern as resources).

 .po file (source)

The file contains translatable strings in standard GNU gettext format:

Edit files with Poedit (free), which compiles the automatically on save.

The file is the binary format read by dxgettext at runtime. It is generated from the file by Poedit or the command-line tool. Always regenerate the after editing the .

The framework file ( ) includes translations for:

 BorderPanel

The node lets you embed custom content around the login form on four regions — above ( ), below ( ), to the left ( ) and to the right ( ). Each region hosts a single child controller (an HtmlPanel for a logo, a ThemeSwitcher, etc.). All four are optional and can be combined freely; undeclared regions collapse.

The form is the centre. / stack above/below the fields within the centre column; / flank that whole centre column as full-height side panels. The title bar and the Login footer (status/error + button) span the full dialog width:

Rendered below the fields at the bottom of the centre column — just above the full-width footer (Login button). Typically support info, disclaimers, or a theme switcher. The South region right-aligns its content:

 WestView / EastView

Rendered to the left and right of the form as full-height side columns — ideal for a vertical logo or branding next to the credentials, instead of stacked on top:

text:
Kitto x allows you to put macros in yaml files. A macro is a symbol that is later expanded to (meaning replaced with) its actual meaning. Macros can be used in place of variables, to make certain parts of your definitions dynamic or context-sensitive. For example, if you wanted to display the current date you would use the macro. If you needed the name of the currently authenticated user, you would use .

 Predefined macros 

A number of macros are predefined, meaning available by default in every Kitto x application. Have a look at the source unit (via Delphi's Help Insight) for the full list.

 Config macros 

You can access the value of any key in Config.yaml (or whatever config file was used to start the application) through the syntax . Slashes are used to descend the yaml hierarchy.

This is useful to set two config keys to the same value without wirting it twice, or to set a view property in terms of a config setting.

 Auth macros 

All authentication data is available as macros in the namespace. Most common among them are and , but you can add your own values by customizing the auth definition in the config file.

A few macros are populated automatically by the framework:

 Macro | Set when | Value |
 
 | After successful login | The user name as authenticated |
 | After successful login | Raw config name of the database connection currently active for this session — either the user's choice from the Environment combo or the configured (e.g. ) |
 | After successful login | User-friendly label of the active database, taken from if defined, falling back to otherwise. Matches the text shown in the login combo, so it is the right macro for the StatusBar or dialog titles |

Custom columns returned by a query are also exposed under the namespace — see Custom User Columns.

 Session macros 

Four macros describe the session and the client it is being served to. They are most often used as a on a model field, to stamp a record with where it came from.

 Macro | Value |
 
 | The server-side session id |
 | The language currently active for the session |
 | The host the client addressed the request to — the header, e.g. |
 | The client's IP address, e.g. or for a local browser |

 warning They only expand while a request is being served
 and describe the client, so they come from the request. Expanding a string that contains them outside a request — at startup, or from a background job — leaves them untouched, and the placeholder itself ends up wherever the value was going. The other two behave the same way with respect to the session.

 Database macros 

Macros in the namespace are expanded by the current DB adapter (more precisely, by the DB engine type associated to the current connection: , , , ). This lets you write a single SQL expression that automatically translates to the right dialect at runtime.

The expansion happens transparently before the SQL command is sent to the database, both for FireDAC, ADO and DBExpress access layers.

text:
Models 

Models in Kitto x represent data. The most common case is a model representing a database table, although other types of models based on database views or more abstract models are possible.

 tip Generate Models from your database
You rarely write Model files from scratch: the Model Wizard reverse-engineers them from your existing database (physical names, references, detail references, labels/hints from column comments), and the Model Editor lets you refine them visually. This page documents the YAML those tools produce.

A model is a yaml file stored under Metadata\Models, and is identified by its name. Here is an example:

 Model properties 

As you can see in the example above, a model is identified by its . In this case, it is simply the name of the underlying database table, but it can be changed. 

A model can also have subnodes with additional attributes. For example:
 : Physical name of the underlying database table or view.
 : by default. Set it to for models that grow with business activity (transactions, accumulating registries, large lookups). Three concrete effects:
 1. List grid auto-load: the List controller defaults to , opening the grid empty until the user applies a filter or clicks Refresh.
 2. List paging: the List controller defaults to , enabling the bottom pager bar and server-side pagination.
 3. Reference editor: a Form field of type renders as a searchable lookup popup instead of a dropdown combo (the dropdown would otherwise have to load every row of a large table into the page).

 Effects 1 and 2 can be overridden per-view via and on the ViewTable.

 Effect 3 can be overridden per Reference field with an explicit , useful when a already narrows the candidate set to a handful of rows that fit better in a dropdown:
 
 Resolution order: view-field → model-field (on the Reference) → referenced model .

 Whichever editor type is chosen (dropdown or popup), selecting a record fires the same server-side cascade and fan-out, so dependent fields (codice fiscale, descrizione, etc.) keep auto-populating consistently.

 : order by clause. It must always be qualified using the standard {Q} qualifier and use fields' physical name
 : condition for filter where clause. It must always be qualified using the standard {Q} qualifier and use fields' physical name.
 : is a user-readable description displayed Used as a label when displaying a single record. If missing, it is synthesized.
 : is a user-readable description displayed as a label when displaying multiple records. If missing, the singular display label is "pluralized".
 : By default, a model is linked to the default database ( ) defined in . You can add the property: 
 
to link it to the database instead. This means that all read and write operations for that model are performed against the database (which must be defined in as well).

A model can also have data validation and business that you declare in the model (and in its fields) and that are enforced at various times. Kitto x includes a number of predefined rule types you can use, and you can add your own in Delphi. See the Business Rules concept page for the full picture.

 Model fields and their properties 

Fields are defined under the node, using a syntax similar to SQL. Every field has a data type, optionally a size (for some data types only), and can be a required field ( ) or not. One or more fields can also be marked as the model's (this is required to make the model data editable).

 Kitto x includes a set of predefined data types, but since a data type is just a Delphi class inherited from , you can add your own. Current data types are String, Memo, HTMLMemo, Integer, Date, Time, DateTime, Boolean, Float, Decimal, Currency plus the special Reference type which represents a reference to another model (the equivalent of a d

Database Routing 

 Kitto x allows you to work with more than one databases at a time through the database routing feature. 

First define in Config.yaml all your databases:

The syntax to do database routing is the following:

you can apply it at Model level or at View level.

 Database routing at the Model level 

The basic use at Model level is explained here:

 Database routing at the View level 

Beside linking a model to a particular database, you can do database routing at the DataView.
This is useful in case you have multiple databases with similar structure and want to define a single model with different views each linked to a different database.

 Other uses of database routing 

Database routing is enabled in other places, always through the same syntax. These places are:

 | For database-based access controllers, defines the database holding the AC data. |
 
 | For database-based authenticators, defines the database holding the auth data (user names and passwords, generally.|
 DynaList filters in a List controller| You can fetch the list of values for a list filter from a different database if nedded. |

Generally, you can use database routing everywhere a database connection is implied.

 Accessing a routed database from Delphi code 

When you write rules, custom tools, or any business code that needs to talk to a non-default database, use — it returns a per-request cached for the named database. The connection is borrowed from the framework cache and released automatically at end of request, so you only free the query or command you create, not the connection itself.

See How to access databases from Delphi code for the full ownership contract, transactional helpers, and the rare cases where is required instead.

 Advanced: Customizing database routing 

All examples of database routing we have seen so far have been using the router, but you can create your own router if you have a dynamic rule that matches models to databases (for example, a naming convention). Creating your own router involves looking into the unit and using the existing router as an example. It all boils down to inheriting a new class from and overriding the method to implement said rule. Your new router can have as many parameters as needed. Everything below the node is passed to the method at run time.

Don't forget to call in your initialization section (and the symmetrical in the finalization section) in order to make your custom database router available to your application.
